speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
ask the Minister of Labour a question arising out of a press report this morning to the effect that a royal commission has been appointed to investigate labour conditions in the British Columbia shipyards. Is that report correct; and what is the occasion for a royal commission when the department has such full powers now under the mobilization and other acts?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA SHIPYARDS- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSION UNDER INQUIRIES ACT
speechtext:
I was just going to make an
announcement on that matter.
A commission has been appointed under the Inquiries Act to inquire into the means of securing maximum production in the British Columbia shipyards. The commission will report on methods of increasing the output of ships, and on a plan for the operation of the yards six days in the week which was submitted by a dfeputation representative of the shipyard employees. Specifically the terms of reference of the commission are:
1.	To examine into the operation of the plan of continuous operation now in effect and to give due consideration to the substitute plan submitted by the deputation.
2.	To inquire into any factors now impeding production in the shipyards of British Columbia and as to the most effective means of securing maximum production in such shipyards.
3.	To report on the foregoing.
Labour Conditions

The chairman of the commission is the Hon. Stephen Ellswood Richards, of Winnipeg. There are two members representing employers and two representing employees. The employer members are Mr. Don Serviss, general manager of North Vancouver Shipyards, and Mr. Hugh Lewis, general manager of South Yard, Burrard Dry Dock, Vancouver. The employee representatives are Mr. Chris. Pritchard, of the United Association of Plumbers and Steamfitters and President of the Metal Trades Council, Vancouver; and Mr. A. A. McAuslane, Vice-President of the Canadian Congress of Labour, Vancouver.
In announcing the appointment of the commission I wish to state that the Minister of Munitions and Supply and myself are resolved that all steps necessary to secure the greatest possible output of ships from the yards in British Columbia shall be taken. No doubt changes in the existing procedures of management and labour will be necessary, but in the present dire need for vessels to carry the tools of war to the battle fronts, nothing can be permitted to stand in the way.
In March I visited the shipyards on the Pacific coast and conferred with representatives of the managements and of the employees. As a result of these conferences a plan was proposed for the continuous operation of the yards. Three shifts were to be established, and operations were to continue twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, but each employee was to have one day of rest in seven. After further conferences I left Vancouver feeling that all parties were agreed on the adoption of this programme. I am glad to be able to say that nine unions, representing about 95 per cent of the employees of the coast shipyards, accepted the plan and entered into supplementary agreements for its adoption. Two unions declined to enter into these agreements, despite a request from the unions that entered into the contract that they should do so. The failure of a small minority group to cooperate in this plan for greater production of ships and, I think I may add, one or two missteps on the part of certain of the managements, prevented the plan being brought into full application. This had a disquieting effect on the members of the unions which did sign the agreement. Members of the non-cooperating unions were not in their places on Sunday, while members of the cooperating unions reported for work with the feeling that they were being subjected to discrimination.
In these confused circumstances a joint * conference of shipyards unions was organized. This body developed an alternative plan for six days operation a week, which, in their view,
rMr. Mitchell.l
would prove as effective in promoting production as the plan of continuous operation. The joint conference of shipyards unions prepared a brief in support of their plan, and a deputation from the conference came to Ottawa to discuss it with me. I met the deputation on June 27 and 29. In these negotiations I was impressed by the sincere desire of the representatives of the shipyards workers to cooperate in any effort which would promote greater ship production. I pointed out, however, that the brief they" had submitted had many implications which would take some time to explore. Obviously I would have to discuss their plan with my colleagues interested in the shipbuilding programme and especially with the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I requested the delegation to urge upon the shipyard employees in British Columbia that they should give the plan of continuous operation a thirty-day trial. I agreed that if this were done, their representations for an alternative scheme would be carefully considered, and my decision would be rendered as nearly as possible within thirty days.
It is very gratifying to me that the members of the deputation entered into this undertaking, and I can now report that all employees in the coast shipyards have accepted the recommendations of their representatives and that the yards are now building ships twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week.
The commission to which I refer will begin its investigations in Vancouver on July 20. I am confident that the members of the commission will concentrate on the one allimportant question of how to build the utmost possible number of ships in the shortest possible time, and that they will submit a constructive report.
I should like to point out to the house that, despite various allegations on the irresponsibility of trade unions, in this case a group of trade unions in a very important industry under the guidance of responsible national leaders have met a crisis in one of the most serious phases of our war effort in an altogether creditable manner. I am confident these men will give Canada all they have to give in the production of ships.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PRODUCTION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA SHIPYARDS- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSION UNDER INQUIRIES ACT
speechtext:
I am
obliged to the minister for having made that statement. The only thought that occurs to me is this: if there has been a complete agreement and there is now full cooperation on the plan suggested by the minister, why a royal commission? What other intervening

Hong Kong Commission
circumstances have made it necessary to issue a commission under the 'Inquiries Act? I do not think the minister made that clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRODUCTION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA SHIPYARDS- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSION UNDER INQUIRIES ACT
speechtext:
I thought I had made that quite clear. When the delegation came to see me I pointed out to them, and I think quite rightly, that it was not sound to say that a seven-day working week in the shipyards was not practicable until it had been tried out. I said to them that first of all, in fairness to the government, and in view of the urgent need of shipping, it should at least be tried out by all the unions engaged in the production of ships in the shipyards of Vancouver. I pointed out that a decision upon their brief, which was a lengthy document, could not be made within a day or two days; it would have to be analysed by some responsible authority. But I promised them that if they gave this plan a trial, as soon as possible, after thirty days I would make decision whether a six-day week, in my opinion or that of the government, was the most practical approach to the problem, or the seven-day week.
May I also point out that this has been called at the coast the Mitchell plan. It is quite true that I had negotiations there with both employers and employees, and I think it is fair to say that the arrangements made were made in pursuance of the negotiations, in that- the employers and the employees in the British Columbia shipyards, seeing the urgency of the situation, agreed to this seven-day operation without any coercion from the federal government. It was unfortunate, I think, that, mistakes having been made by certain employers and certain trade unions, the plan was not given the trial which in my judgment was necessary in view of the desperate situation in which this nation and all the united nations are placed at the moment with respect to shipping to carry the products of this country, both food and war materials, to those who are really fighting the battle of democracy and of freedom.

"10. Chocolate, candy and confectionery which may be classed as candy or a substitute for

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Last night when the committee rose the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) and myself, had made certain representations with regard to candy that was being retailed at one cent. Has the minister considered whether or not it is possible to reduce the tax on candy selling for one cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A great deal of consideration was given this question last week, and it has received further consideration since the representations were made in committee last night. The situation is this. The 30 per cent tax as it stands applies to all candies at the manufacturers level, and my information is that about 8 per cent of the candy manufactured is sold for sale in one-cent units. No company that I know of sells candy in one-cent units alone. Some companies sell a larger proportion of their output in that form than do others, and representations have been made by those companies that have the largest proportion of their output in one-cent units. The inevitable effect of relieving part of the output of the candy industry of Canada from the 30 per cent tax would be to divert a larger proportion of the manufacture into that particular form of output. Indeed, it is altogether likely that the one cent part of the output would be advertised as free from taxation. Consideration has been given as to measures by which that diversion, which would be unfair, undesirable and expensive to the treasury, could be prevented, and we have not been able to satisfy ourselves that any measures that could be taken would be entirely effective. The objection that was made last night was that this wmuld mean that units now selling for one cent would hereafter sell for more-perhaps two for three, or three for four, or four for five, or something of the kind. [Mr. IlsIey.J
This increase in the price would not be permitted by the wartime prices and trade board. In the budget it was clearly stated that increases that were necessitated by this tax would be permitted by the wartime prices and trade board. A limited range of articles was selected, and the policy was clearly laid down that these increases would be permitted. It is true that the 30 per cent increase in price as applied to the one cent article comes to a fractional figure, one cent and a fraction, and in that case it would be necessary for the retailer to sell for two cents unless he combined several units and sold two for three, or three for four, or four for five, and my information is that to do so would be regarded by the wartime prices and trade board as objectionable.
It may be said that the dampening effect of this tax on the sale of candy in one-cent units will bring about much distress to candy manufacturers who are heavily in the manufacture of one-cent units, and to retailers heavily interested in selling them. This might be true under normal conditions. I am informed that many years ago-I do not know how many

a candy tax such as this, or of some kindi, was proposed, and abandoned because it would be unfair to the sellers of one-cent candies. But under present conditions I am not convinced that there would be much injury. There may be a little; that is a necessary result of many of our measures. But the reason why there will not be much injury is that sugar is severely rationed. Candy manufacturers are permitted to use only 70 per cent of their normal supply, and they can sell without any trouble all the candy they make. The manufacturer whose output is 50 per cent in one-cent units and 50 per cent in larger units will perhaps find that the one-cent part of his output will be reduced, but he will sell more of the other. It will render some little adjustment necessary, but it will not have the serious effect that there might be if there were a scramble for a market, or if it were difficult to sell the output, when the loss would not be compensated by the increased sale of another type of output.
On the whole, therefore, I am inclined to think that the tax should stand as it is. The argument that was used last night was as to the children. The hon. member for Trinity argued that it is not for us to judge; that the children want to buy one-cent sticks of candy and we ought to let them do so. It all depends on how important one considers these things. I do not think it would be a great hardship on the people of this country if the children had to pay three cents for two sticks of candy instead of one cent for one. I cannot

Special War Revenue Act
get much worked up over that. We should be careful not to work any injustice on the manufacturers and retailers, but I do not think the adverse effect of this tax will be at all substantial. On the other hand if we make this exception for one part of the output of the candy factories we are going to have similar demands as regards chewing gum, and we would be called upon to exercise very fine discretion as to how far we could go in that regard. It certainly sets a precedent that I want to avoid if at all possible. If for instance the diversion, as a result of exempting part of the output of the candy factories from this 30 per cent tax, would be that 16 per cent of the total output instead of 8 per cent went into one-cent pieces-that is, if it were doubled, which would be quite possible unless we could take counter measures, the practicability of which is disputed by those who advise me-it would mean a loss of revenue of between $500,000 and $600,000.

I have no brief for the candy manufacturers but, I have for the small corner store owner. Last night several hon. members mentioned the big firms. They can buy and sell at reduced prices, but the corner grocery store man is in a tight spot with the wartime prices and trade board regulations. In a check-up it was found that some of these corner stores near schools will lose about five per cent of their trade owing to this one-cent candy being cut out. That sounds like a lot, but these storekeepers claim that if the children do not come to their stores to buy the candy, then when it comes to buying other and more expensive articles the families will go to other stores and take the trade away from the small stores. Last week there was an article in the Ottawa Journal regarding one-cent candy, and it said that relief was to be given to the corner grocery store. Did the minister see that article?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What kind of relief?

It did not say-just that relief was to be given to the corner grocery in regard to this one-cent candy. The small storekeeper is the one who is going to feel it, and he has a tough time now. When he has to buy a bag of sugar he has to gather 40 one-pound coupons, bundle them up and take them to his wholesaler. The wholesaler is in the same fix; when he wants to buy a car of sugar he has to have 40,000 of these one-pound coupons. I have a letter here from a firm which states that it means counting out 40,000 tickets to get a car of sugar; they may sell three cars a month, so that they have to have an extra clerk to look after the details of these transactions alone.
The storekeeper is in the same position. He is selling less and less every day, and this one-cent candy wrould help him out.
As to the cards that are sent out by the wartime prices and trade board urging people to save sugar, in most cases they are thrown into the wastepaper basket. There has been more sugar sold since the rationing went into effect than when people were on the honour system.

I protest against this tax on the one-cent candy business. I realize that all the people of Canada should make some sacrifice to help win the war, and everyone is ready to do it, but why put it on the children's one-cent candy? The leader of the opposition pointed out yesterday that the province of Quebec is interested in this. We have many manufacturers of one-cent candy. Really the one-cent candy is an institution for our children in the province of Quebec. I do not see why we should impose a tax which would have the effect of ruining that industry. Some hon. members said yesterday that it is doubtful whether candy or sugar is good for children. It is like everything else; if they eat too much it is not good for them, but sugar is necessary in the diet of children. So far as the one-cent candy is concerned there should be no tax on it, to help the children and to help the manufacturers.

I look on this as a very
undesirable way of raising revenue. I think that is the main purpose of this provision- to raise revenue, rather than to restrict the sale of chocolates. Whatever the motive or objective of the proposal, the result is an inflation of price. In the past the minister has pointed out that one way of reducing the purchasing power of the people is by inflation, but he has deplored that method. In past months and years, he has wept crocodile tears over the tremendous dangers of inflation; yet by this very legislation we are now bringing about inflation of prices in order to curtail the purchasing power of the people, in this case the purchasing power of the children. I do not think the minister is being consistent in his attitude. If it is necessary to curtail the purchasing power. of the children, or of the people generally, so that they will buy less commodities, surely the only sound way of doing it is by a more direct form of taxation. If on the other hand the objective is to restrict the sale of chocolates, then I would say the logical way to do it would be by rationing. Nevertheless I point out again that whatever the objective may be, the result is nothing more or less than inflation, the very thing the minister has been warning the country against for years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I desire
to add a word or two to what I said last evening on this question. I have now had the opportunity of reading the proposed amendment which was moved last night with respect to small packaged goods, which I think refers not only to 'bare but to other items retailing ordinarily at 5, 10 and 15 cents. Originally the minister proposed to impose a tax of 30 per cent ad valorem on the manufacturers' prices. Now he has changed that to a specific tax of one cent, two cents and three cents, as the case may be, to be added to the retail price of the five-, ten- and fifteen-cent packages. I assume that this will meet the objections advanced by the manufacturers to the imposition of the 30 per cent tax. Under some arrangement the retailer will be allowed to add the tax to the retail price. The effect of that, of course, will be to reduce somewhat the volume of that business, but as I see it-and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong-this overcomes the difficulty which would have been experienced in maintaining the price ceiling and at the same time giving effect to the new' taxation. I hope that deduction is correct; if it is, I should think half the objection to the proposals would be eliminated, because I am informed that the so-called bar and small package business amounts to 50 per cent of the whole production of the country. So much for that, if I have the correct understanding.
With respect to penny goods, so-called, I am told that these represent only about 8 per cent of the total production of the manufacturers of the country. I believe that is the representation that has been made to the minister. Perhaps that includes gum; I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not arguing the case for the gum people. They may be able to meet the situation in another way, by reducing the amount of the gum, for instance. In any case I am not arguing that matter, because I have not had any information on the subject. There may be great merit in any complaints they make, but I am not attempting to deal with that point to-day.
The penny goods may amount to much more than 8 per cent of the production of some manufacturers, and much less in the case of others. With regard to those in the latter class, of course if this proposal goes into effect and the price becomes two for three cents, undoubtedly there will be some reduction in the volume of trade which will affect the small comer grocery and candy shop much more
[Mr. Quelch.I
than anyone else. I think the greatest detriment will be to the small candy stores in our cities and towns, near the schools, and so on. But the total volume is small, and it does seem to me the amount of revenue that would be received from this tax also would be relatively small. I think the minister could well forgo that revenue, because in the cost to the country the increase otherwise will be relatively very large. The minister says he is not concerned about the children. Well, in the end it is the parents who have to pay. People become accustomed to candy. Three cents may not be a very large sum of money, but I remember very well that when I was a boy one cent was all we were ever handed, and when I reached the stage when I was given a nickel or a dime I really thought I was a millionaire. I am afraid that condition does not obtain to-day; people hand out money to their children much more freely than in days gone by, and perhaps that is wrong. But I do suggest to- the minister that in justice to the industry, and more particularly in justice to the small retailer, he could very well forgo the tax on the penny goods.
The chocolate bar situation has been taken care of, and I believe that amounts to about 50 per cent of the w'hole business. I am told that business is growing, I think largely due to the purchases made by the young men in the armed forces, who do not get enough sugar in their food and who buy these bars in quantities. If the minister would forgo this tax, which affects about 8 per cent of the total business, that would leave about 42 per cent of the trade, which is distributed over all the other varieties of candy. With respect to the higher class goods, which ordinarily sell in fancy boxes at a dollar a pound, I think in days gone by 1 had the figures with regard to the total production in Canada, though I do not recall them now; but during the depression period the volume of that high-class candy was very materially reduced. People did not buy it; they just did not have the money. I am not asking anything for the people who buy that class of goods; I think they can pay the tax, which I believe runs around 18 cents a pound on certain qualities. Perhaps that situation can be met in large measure by reducing the cost of the package. We see these beautiful ornate candy boxes in the windows, which occasionally young men buy for their girl friends. I hear now that cigarettes are the appropriate thing to give your girl friend, but it was not so when I was a boy. We bought candy for our girls when we were courting. The manufacturers can reduce this cost very largely by cutting down these unnecessary expenses, and they should be cut down. There will be a

Special War Revenue Act
loss to the manufacturer, but he is not complaining about that. He is operating under pretty difficult circumstances, with the reduction in the quantity of sugar he may use, but as a rule he is a patriotic citizen and he will carry on. The sugar tax has hit him hard in the past, and he has not always been able to pass that on. During the depression he passed very little of it on, and none of these companies has made a dollar since 1930. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

The present proposal is really a species of inflation, since the price is going to be six cents instead of five cents.

The minister has suggested that the penny candies should be sold two pieces for three cents instead of a cent apiece. With, the new tax this candy will cost the manufacturers sixty-eight cents, and if they abide by the price ceiling regulations they will have to sell it for seventy-two cents. The increase is all going one way. I do not know who is going to absorb this tax, the manufacturer
or the retailer. If the retailer is to be allowed to increase his price, the manufacturer should be entitled to do the same. As other hon. members have said, candy is a necessity for children, even though it is not so necessary for grown-ups. There should be some way of arranging it so that the youngsters can get their candy when they need it, even if it be necessary to cut out the manufacture of the higher grade candy.

I urge upon the minister and his officers that this tax on penny goods be reconsidered. I think we all admit that candy is really a children's food; most adults would be a great deal better off if they did not have it. The minister says that to eliminate the tax on penny goods would reduce his revenue. Bar candy represents about 50 per cent of the output of candy in Canada. A tax of one cent per unit is now being imposed, in place of the 30 per cent basis, this means an increase of 9 per cent. A 9 per cent increase on 50 per cent of the candy output would offset the revenue that would be lost if this tax on penny goods were not, imposed. Chocolate bars will continue to be used, because they are handy to buy and fit the needs of pretty nearly everybody. I am not concerned about the retailers or the manufacturers or anyone else; I am concerned only about the children. After all, this is the children's food; with the rationing of sugar there will be fewer cakes made in the homes, and the only way the children will be able to make up this deficiency will be by buying penny goods. I believe if the minister and his officers carefully consider this matter they wall realize that they could offset any loss of revenue by imposing a higher tax on the higher grade candies.

Much has been said about children needing candy. All persons need a considerable amount of sugar in one form or another, because sugar is the great energizing food of the human race. It does not make any difference whether people take this food in the form of sugar or in the form of candy. The very fact that sugar has been rationed and there is only a limited quantity of it available in the household is one of the best arguments against a tax upon candy. What has brought about this increased consumption of candy? In the days of prohibition candy took the place of alcohol. In the normal process of digestion sugar is changed into alcohol, and when a man could not get that commodity his natural taste and inclination was toward an increased consumption of sugar. The fact that sugar is rationed will stop many

people from making home-made candy, and the children will have to buy candy at the stores. Sugar is a necessary food and should be part of the daily diet of every person, either in that form or in the form of candy. To put a tax upon candy is like putting a tax upon bread. I ask the minister to reconsider the whole question of the tax on candy. While the measure proposed may be productive of some revenue, I think any good will be counteracted by the harm it will actually do to the people of this country.

The minister should reconsider this matter, because the present proposal if it is adopted will work a hardship, not only upon our children but upon the small storekeepers. Some people say that candy is injurious to children's teeth, but it is not the candy that does the harm; it is a lack of milk and calcium. This will be found among the poorer children. The resolution proposes
certain changes in our existing tax on insurance premiums, and in addition imposes a premium tax on life insurance as a result of the provincial agreements. The committee may recall that when I announced the offer to the provincial governments I said that if it were accepted it might subsequently be necessary for the dominion government to levy certain taxes in order to prevent some groups from securing an undue advantage as a result of relief from provincial taxes. It was found in the case of insurance companies that certain additional taxes might properly be imposed. Generally speaking, the dominion government is levying a 2 per cent tax in place of the provincial taxes, which on the average were slightly above this figure. At the same time, we have used this occasion for making minor changes in our own taxes applying to ordinary stock, fire and casualty companies. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Previously the mutual companies paid one per cent on their premiums. Those companies were free from income tax, and therefore there was no possibility of deducting the premium tax from their income tax. That was not true of the stock companies. The stock companies paid one per cent on their premiums, but there was a provision that they could deduct that from their income tax. If they are paying income tax-and every company that is not making a loss is paying income tax-they will continue paying what they were before; that is to say, they will be paying that much more income tax.

Previously they paid one per cent in premium taxes, subtracting that from the income tax. Now that one per cent, is taken out altogether and they just pay the income tax, which will be the same amount in taxation, provided they are making profits, which they are. But that is not true in the case of the mutual, fire and casualty companies, and in order to maintain the same relative position that existed before it is therefore necessary to levy the one per cent which was always on the mutual company premiums and add two per cent to that. In the case of fire insurance companies the one per cent is taken out of the act, for the purpose of simplicity more than anything else; so that the result is that you have two per cent on premiums of stock companies and three per cent on premiums of mutual companies. There are some
representations I should like to make, particularly concerning trunks, watches, tobacco pipes and fountain pens. These items are particularly necessary for the men in service. So far as the officer is concerned it is necessary for him to secure a trunk. As to these other items, they are not luxuries for the men in the armed forces; they are necessities. To-day the position of officers, particularly in Canada, who are on active service, is that their outfit allowance does not cover the extra expenditures which will have to be made should this tax go into effect. To-day they are not exempted from income tax in Canada. I personally believe the officers on active service in Canada, in whatever branch, should be exempt, but that is beside the point at the moment. These items, however, are necessities, and under this section the men in the services and their relatives and friends will have to contribute the major portion of the amount that will be realized from the imposition of this tax. Other people are not buying them, as the leader of the opposition points out. The items I have mentioned are absolute necessities for the men in service, and are purchased either by them or by their relatives. I am going to make the suggestion to the minister that these items be exempted from the tax. I realize that the minister will point out the difficulties in administration, but I think any difficulties of that kind could be obviated by having the man in the service who purchases any of these things for use in the service swear to a declaration to that effect, and if his relatives or friends wish to make him gifts of that kind, they in turn could swear to the necessary declarations pointing out that the recipient was to be a man in uniform.
The minister has consistently refused to accept suggestions for changes in the regulations, and we have come to take it for granted that regardless of what representations may be made, they will not be accepted. But I

think this is one representation, very much along the line of representations made here earlier to-d'ay, which could be accepted. It is absolutely necessary that an officer have a trunk. If it costs $25 or $30, you are adding another $10 to his cost. If a sendee man buys a watch it is subject to a 25 per cent tax; if he buys a fountain pen or a pipe, he has to pay a 35 per cent tax. It would be a nice gesture on the part of the minister, as well as a very considerable benefit to the men in service both here and abroad, if this exemption should be granted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That opens up the whole question of how far we should go in granting taxation exemptions to men in the service. I must say that I am very reluctant to shoot our whole taxation system full of holes on these grounds. If men in the service are not receiving sufficient remuneration, that is a matter that should be considered and is considered from time to time; but to give them special consideration through a series of tax remissions is in my judgment wrong in principle.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have done it, have we not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, yes. I should be very much surprised, however, to find that Great Britain does it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I believe they do not, nor does the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no exemption even in the case of income tax; everybody pays it in Great Britain, whether he is in the army or not. Last year when we were discussing the motion picture tax, for example, I believe one hon. member, I have forgotten who it was, suggested that men in the sendee going to the motion pictures should not have to pay that tax. The suggestion did not meet with any favour, but it would be the logical result of granting taxation exemptions to those in the armed forces. With regard to travel on the railways by members of the forces, we did make an exemption. There seemed to be a particularly good reason for it, because we were taking those men long distances from their homes, and if they wanted to go home they were obliged to use the railways, so that perhaps there was some reason for that. Personally I am averse to adding to the list of exemptions from taxes, and I should be surprised if there was very much demand for it. I do not think we should take our taxation system and wherever possible say, "This should not apply to members of the armed forces." The adjustment there should be in pay rather than exemptions from this, that and the other tax.

The minister's explanation is that it would be unfair to exempt any particular group, yet the amendment to section 15 provides for doing so. It says:

Personally I cannot see the argument advanced by the minister, particularly in view of the proviso he added to section 15 last evening.

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may say that resolution No. 5 is to be dropped.
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act and to provide-
1.	That superannuation benefits granted by the dominion, the provinces or any superannuation or pension fund or plan shall be subject to succession duty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is proposed to add a section to the succession duty act to make superannuation benefits granted by the dominion, the provinces or any superannuation or pension fund or plan subject to succession duty. This, I think, is a departure in principle from anything which has obtained heretofore. I do not believe it is in effect in any of the provinces. I should like to be informed on that point. If I understand the superannuation law correctly, the allowance paid to the widow of a deceased civil servant is equal to one-half of what the deceased would be entitled to receive. To each child under eighteen years of age an allowance is paid of 10 per cent of what the deceased was entitled to receive, but this is not to exceed 8300 per annum. The allowances paid to all children shall not exceed the allowance to the widow, and the total allowance to the widow and the children shall not exceed 75 per cent of the allowance to which the civil servant would have been entitled. In other words, for the remainder of her life the widow will receive one-half the superannuation to which her husband would have been entitled, while each child under the specified age will receive 10 per cent. Is it proposed to capitalize these annuity payments to the widow and children?
I use that term for lack of a better word. Is this done in any other jurisdiction? Where will they get the money to pay this levy? In the case of the dominion superannuation fund I suppose it could be taken out of the hides of the widow and the children. It could be deducted at the source.
I am wondering about the equity of this proposal. Part of these payments is contributed by the civil servant during his service and part is contributed by the government.

Succession Duty Act
There is practically no management of the fund, because it exists only in the books of the nation. We have not a sound superannuation system because we do not have any investments bearing interest. It is just a bookkeeping entry, and I always thought it was deficient in that regard. However, that is the system, and I do not think this is the best time to change it. What is the equity of taxing these payments? Do civil servants get so rich during their lifetime that they come within the category of men whose estates must pay succession duty? I should like to know the justification for this new form of taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sure whether the provinces tax this, but I believe they do. These superannuation payments to the widow and children I submit are within the spirit of the act which taxes annuities, insurance moneys and benefits of the kind which pass on the death of the deceased. There would be no question about the taxability of superannuation payments if the Civil Service Superannuation Act provided that the government "shall" pay the widow and the children so much per year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What does it provide?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It provides that the government "may" pay the widow and children, and the point has been raised that that makes it a discretionary payment and does not entitle the widow as a right to receive anything.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is
the practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The practice is always to pay. Using the word "may" instead of "shall" is a mere technicality. There may have been instances-I have no knowledge of any-where the government has refused to pay for some reason or another, but certainly every man in the service thinks that his wife and children are protected by his superannuation payments and regards the superannuation payments as just as safe as an annuity provided under a life insurance policy, which would be taxable. Therefore, it was thought that this should be put beyond any doubt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On the theory that this is a capital asset?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do not need to say that it is a capital asset. It is property.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is
property passing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a succession.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is done only because the legislature declares it to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is it
necessary to do it? I can imagine cases where a superannuated civil servant left an estate of X dollars to his wife and children which, under the exemptions in the succession duty act, without the evaluation of this annuity to his wife and children, would not be liable to any taxation at all. There are border-line cases where, by the evaluation of the annuity, which the minister in one case at least has designated as a contract with the civil servant and treating it as property passing, the value of the estate would be raised above the amount of the exemption, and the whole estate would thereupon become liable to pay succession duties. That is a. pretty rough kind of legislation, and I would like to know the reason for it. Evaluating the annuity might just tip the scale by $50 and make the whole estate liable to pay a tremendous amount of duty. I do not think this is just. If the retiring allowance were large, and the widow were young and the children under eighteen, the evaluation of the annuity might be quite substantial. I am trying to visualize the border-line cases where the evaluation might just tip the scale and result in a very substantial sum being taken from the estate. I deprecate this, and I wonder why it is being done. It was not formerly done in provincial statutes. I do not know what the provincial law is now, because I have not looked at the statutes for two or three years. What is the occasion for this amendment? Why was it not done last year if it was the proper thing to do? What has drawn it to the attention of the department now? Have there been cases where it would be unjust not to tax? I think we ought to be told the story behind the story of this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be unfair and indefensible in my judgment to tax annuities which were purchased by the deceased and which might just tip the scale to taxability of the estate, and also to tax insurance moneys provided by the deceased, and not to tax the superannuation payments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We are
accustomed to taxation upon insurance moneys.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Suppose a critic of our legislation were to point out that whoever drafted this act had very carefully left out such a provision as this so that civil servants got
Succession Duty Act

away without paying any succession duties on their superannuation, while for the rank and file of people all over the country any annuity which is provided for the widow and children makes the estate taxable. What would the answer be? I do not think there could be any answer. I think it is only fair that these superannuation pensions, because that is what they are, annuities, should be treated the same as other annuities, the same as insurance payments, and I am sure that the public would be of that opinion. There would be no doubt at all about the matter if the word "shall" were used instead of "may" in the Civil Service Superannuation Act. Why "may" was used I do not know, but I presume it was used on the theory that "may" is the word that ought to be used when obligations are saddled upon the crown, or something of that kind. I think there is a recent case in which it was decided that these payments are not taxable because of the use of the word "may." I think that is the reason for the legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How
much does the minister expect to get out of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know.

Is the change applicable to
other pension funds such as those of the railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are taxed now.

This change is to apply
only to governmental annuities and superannuation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
It seems to be broader than that because it says "any superannuation or pension fund or plan." Are these words meant to apply only to a governmental plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are being inserted
because governmental plans were in mind. If the act does not cover these other funds, it will now. But I think it does already. It was thought by the draughtsmen and by myself that the act covered superannuation payments, and I was very much surprised to learn that it did not.

That is under section 3 (I)
(g) of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And (h). Section 3 (I)
(g) of the act states:
A "succession" shall be deemed to include the following dispositions of property and the beneficiary and the deceased shall be deemed to be the "successor" and "predecessor" respectively in relation to such property:-
(g) any annuity or other interest purchased or provided by the deceased, either by himself [Mr. Ilsleyd
alone or in concert or by arrangement with any other person, to the extent of the beneficial interest accruing or arising by survivorship or otherwise on the death of the deceased.
I certainly thought that included superannuation payments, and when I learned that it did not, by reason of some opinion or some court decision-I think there was a court decision-I said that the act would have to be amended at once to ensure that superannuation payments were included, because otherwise there would be a discrimination in favour of civil servants against the rank and file of the people of this country.

If the widow of a civil
servant remarries, do the superannuation payments cease?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that I cannot
give that information, but it will be found, I think, in the Civil Service Superannuation Act..

It makes it difficult to
calculate the capital value of the annuity when you have a hazardous condition like that, and sometimes you might be taking an unfair advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The same is true with respect to many wills under which payments to the widow cease upon remarriage.
How do you calculate the capital value of an annuity to a widow which ceases if she remarries?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have had that problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed there would
have to be a refund.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have
had that problem, and I have never been able to find a solution. Take the case of a widow with an annuity of $5,000 which is Cut in half if she remarries. I never knew just how to deal with it, but I always advised the widow that if she did remarry she would lose one-half or three-quarters of her income, as the case might be, and that had a salutary effect,
I think the minister has made a case for this amendment,

Under the act as
it now stands, railway employees are not subject to succession duty, are they? The pertinent sections which were mentioned by the minister were (g) and (h), and I cannot see that either would apply at all to the situation of an employee, for instance, in the railway service who upon discontinuance of his services with the company would be

Succession Duty Act
in receipt of a pension and who subsequently dies. As at present constituted, the act does not cover that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does his widow get a pension then?
I think she gets a pension.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think she does.
I am sure widows do, and this amendment goes a long way farther than is apparent on the face of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it not an annuity provided by the deceased?

It is not in the form of an annuity. It is really a pension scheme. What this amendment actually means is that the widows of all these men, employees, who heretofore have not been subject to succession duty, will now find themselves in the position of being subject thereto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But is not the pension payable yearly in the instance mentioned by the hon. gentleman? If it is payable yearly, it is an annuity.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are payable monthly as a rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The matter can be cleared up simply by what occurred during the past year. There must have been instances where railway employees have been deceased. Has succession duty been charged on the amounts received by the widow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That course has been followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The widow gets $20,000 exemption under our act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commissioner tells me that it is included. He does not remember particular individual cases, but they certainly would be treated as subject to the provisions of the act.

A returned soldier 100 per cent disabled receives $100 a month, as I understand it. In the event of his death his widow then receives $60 a month. Will she have to pay succession duty on a capitalization of $60 a month?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: She will if he leaves over $20,000 or whatever it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The succession is governed by the act, but I would point out that there is a partial exemption in the case of persons who die of wounds inflicted, accident occurring, or disease contracted while Canada is or was at war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What section is that in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is section 7, subsection 3.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is special consideration there?
For the returned soldier and the widow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; not a complete exemption. necessarily, but the act is made very much more lenient with regard to the cases covered by that subsection.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Have any cases arisen out of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not that I can find out.

In the case of these exemptions from succession duties I understand the amount for a widow is $20,000. How do you compute the value of a superannuation or a monthly allotment as of a certain value? Is it amortized?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is an internationally used table which is applied. I cannot give the committee at the moment the name of the table-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -or the rate of interest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

You took the present value of his estate, assuming that he would have lived to the normal expectancy, and then you used the base rate of 3 per cent, which I thought was a very unfair rate to have used, last year. If that is the policy of
Succession Duty Act

the department, I feel sure it would be at least as severe in this case, which is perhaps not as deserving a ease as the other.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I want to ask a question along the lines of the one I asked a few moments ago. If a returned soldier with 100 per cent disability dies, and his widow receives 860 a month or $720 a year, at a 3 per cent rate, if that were capitalized, it would amount to $24,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to the question which was asked by the hon. member for Davenport, I am not sure whether that is an annuity provided by the deceased within the meaning of section 3 (g), and the question has not arisen. I shall have to give that some little consideration before I give an answer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Certainly if the widow under such circumstances is to pay a succession duty, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred it would be most unfair to require her to do so, because, under present conditions. these people have a terrific struggle to get along on the pensions they are receiving.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Could the point not stand for the moment? We could pass this resolution and, when the bill comes before the house, the amendment that is foreshadowed will be placed before the house and will be debated. I will read it then.

2.	That one-half of the estate may be given to charitable organizations in Canada free of succession duty.

Some time ago a gentleman told me that he intended leaving a considerable sum of money to some institution or board which looks after the blind. He wanted his money to go to some charitable institution of that kind. Suppose he left $20,000 for the use of the blind after his death; would one-half of that $20,000 come under the succession duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the instance suggested by the hon. member the whole bequest would be free of succession duty up to one-half of the estate. If the estate were $40,000, or more, a bequest of $20,000 to charity would be entirely free of succession duty.

Then I should have said $40,000, because I did not notice that up to $40,000 was exempt.

Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not right. I was merely trying to accommodate myself to my hon. friend's figures, but there is no $20,000 or $40,000 in the act.

Would one-half of
$20,000 be exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the act was passed last year, half of every charitable bequest is subject to succession duty and half is free. It will be found by reference to Hansard that I did not realize that was what was being done, and I do not think that the committee or the house did. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will it
be made retroactive? It should be if that is the basis of this amendment.

That is very good; I am glad to hear that. The position is this. The act provides, by section 7 (1) (d):
In determining the dutiable value of any property included in a succession, the following exemptions shall be allowed and no duty shall be leviable in respect thereof:
(d) Where the successor is a charitable organization in Canada operated exclusively as such and not for the benefit, gain or profit of any person, member or shareholder thereof, provided that in the case of any property devised or bequeathed by the will of the deceased this exemption shall only apply to an amount not exceeding 50 per centum in the value of such property.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend tne Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, and to provide-
1. That the rates of tax as set out in the second schedule to the said act he repealed and the following substituted therefor:
First part-
Ten per centum of the profits of corporations and joint stock companies and 15 per centum of the profits of all persons other than corporations, before deduction therefrom of any tax paid thereon under the Income War Tax Act.
Second part

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
One hundred per centum of the excess profits.
Third part

speakerposition: stagedirection
