speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is a very difficult, technical taxation measure. The whole question of excess profits is difficult enough, and I confess that from the minister's statement in the budget I was not able to understand all that he was driving at, in two particulars: first, the changes in the base of the E.P.T., as it is called, and second, the question of the refundable portion, to be found in resolution 5. Would the minister please state just what the present position is up to the point where he leaps from 75 per

Excess Profits Tax Act
cent to 100 per cent of the excess profits, and then what the change is? There has been a change on the way up, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Put it on
the record anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The present rate structure of the Excess Profits Tax Act provides for either
(a)	a tax of 22 per cent on total profits, or (b) a tax of 75 per cent on excess profits, whichever is the greater. Under this rate structure it works out that the 75 per cent tax on excess profits is the greater of the two taxes when profits have increased by slightly more than 56 per cent of standard profits. All companies paid at least 40 per cent tax on total profits; that is, 18 per cent under the income tax, and 22 per cent under the Excess Profits Tax Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Under two parts? Is it not in two bites?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The 18 per cent was under the Income War Tax Act, and the 22 per cent was under the Excess Profits Tax Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The 10 per cent under the first part and the 12 per cent under the third?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; I am talking about the
[DOT]old act.
If, however, profits were more than 156 per cent of the standard-the correct figure is 156-7 -then the effective rate of tax on additional profits amounted to 79-5 per cent. Under the new rate structure the 22 per cent has been broken down into a tax of 12 per cent, which applies to total profits in all cases, while the remaining 10 per cent constitutes the tax which is the alternative to the tax on excess profits which was previously 75 per cent but which now becomes 100 per cent.
I have stated that the alternative taxes under the present set-up are equal when a company's profits have increased by just over 56 per cent. Under the proposed rates the alternative taxes are equal when profits have increased by only 16J per cent. It is obvious then that the proposed changes in the rate structure bring into effect the high rate on excess profits at a much lower point than is done in the present law.
To sum up the proposal, I may say that all corporate profits will be taxed at least 40 per cent; and when profits are increased more than 16$ of standard profits, the whole of this excess is taken under the 100 per cent rate, with the 20 per cent refund provision provided for in resolution 4.
In the case of taxpayers other than corporations the 15 per cent flat rate tax remains unaltered as the alternative to the new rate of 100 per cent on excess profits.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was going on to ask the minister if he would give a concrete illustration such as I received to-day from one of the officers of the department, we will say based on a tax on $17,000, which happens to be the figure given, and spread it on the record in tabulated form: first, under the old system; second, under the proposed system, which would show exactly how much tax there would be under the old system, and how the tax was made up in the new system and what it will be. It seems to me that that would be valuable to everyone.

When the minister is putting such an example on the record-I am sure there are very few hon. members who understand exactly how this works out, and I have not had an opportunity to produce practical examples-would he give sufficient examples to illustrate the position of a company which has a fairly steady profit as related to its standard base, and also companies showing very large gains as a result of working on some war contracts?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This, of course, is corporations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will explain in my own words the change that has been made. It is a very technical matter and, if I make a mistake in the course of the explanation, I shall have to correct it to-morrow. I do not think, however, that I shall make a mistake because I am fairly familiar with the legislation from the beginning.
First, let me tell the committee the rule that is applied in ascertaining the taxes payable under the Excess Profits Tax Act now before it is amended. There is an 18 per cent tax under the Income War Tax Act. That is the first thing to remember. Then there is the excess profits tax. Profits are taxed at 75 per cent, and1 there is a provision that the amount in any event shall not be less than 22 per cent of the total profits. That is to say, you must determine whether 75 per cent of the excess, - after deduction of the 18 per cent income tax on the excess, is greater than 22 per cent on the total profits. If it is greater, then one takes the 75 per cent on the excess, w-hich means 79J per cent on the excess if the 18 per cent income tax is first taken into account. The result is that every company must pay at least 40 per cent on its total profits-18 per cent under the Income War Tax Act and1 22 per cent under the
<4561-266

Excess Profits Tax Act

Excess Profits Tax Act-and some companies will pay more than that. If their excess profits are so large that this 79J per cent on the excess is greater than the 22 per cent on the total profits, then they will pay 79J per cent on the excess. One could imagine a company where the two would be exactly equal, and as a matter of fact a company which earns in the taxation year 156-7 per cent of its standard profits would pay exactly the same under both rules.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the point at which they balance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the point at which the two rules bring the same result; 79=j per cent of the excess is equal to 22 per cent of the total profits. So that in practice a very simple rule is applied. One just finds out what the percentage of the company's profits is of its standard profits. If its profits are anything up to 156-7 per cent of its standard profits, one just takes 40 per cent of the profits and that is the tax; that is the combined tax, income and excess profits tax. But if its profits are more than 156-7 per cent of the standard profits, one has to take 40 per cent of the 156-7 per cent and 79J per cent on the remainder over that. That is a simple rule which is applied under the present system to the working out of the taxation on companies. That 156-7, in the minds of chartered accountants, lawyers, income tax officials, and finance department officials, is a well known point; it is the breaking point, the critical point. It is an important figure. Now we have come along and changed our act so that instead of there being an 18 per cent flat rate on all profits, there is now a 30 per cent rate on all profits, which is described in the budget speech as 18 per cent income tax and 12 per cent excess profits tax. But whatever it is called, it is a 30 per cent rate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the total in any event?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Does that apply to anything under $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; according to the resolutions it does. With regard to the option, instead of 22 per cent of the total, or 79J per cent of the excess, whichever is greater, now it is 10 per cent of the total or 100 per cent- of the excess, which ever is greater. So that now every company pays at least 40 per cent of its profits, but it may pay more. For the purposes of the record I will stop

there. The rates are now such that the breaking point, instead of being 156-7 is 116-666, and, therefore the simple rule to apply7 to the computation of the new excess profits tax is to reckon 40 per cent if the company earns less than 116-6 per cent of its standard profits. The simple rule is to take 40 per cent of total profits; but if it earns more than that, one takes 40 per cent up to 116-6 and 100 per cent if it is over, and of the 100 per cent 20 per cent is returnable. That 20 per cent does not apply to excess over standard profits but excess over 116-6 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Twenty per cent of that and that alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Twenty per cent of that and that alone. I have seen some recapitulations of this in business papers and, as usual, there is some misunderstanding. I am not surprised, but there is a misunderstanding. It seems to be thought that 20 per cent of the excess over 100 per cent is returnable. It is only 20 per cent of the excess over 116-66 per cent.
That is a brief explanation of the new measure, and the best I can give. It will be seen that since 40 per cent of any profits are taken and 100 per cent over 116-66 per cent, the most any company has left is 70 per cent of its standard profits, because 40 per cent of 116-6 is 46-6, which, subtracted from 116-6, leaves 70. So that the most any company can have left available for dividends under this measure is 70 per cent of its standard profits. It may have in addition a credit with the government of the 20 per cent excess. If it earns more than 116-6 per cent of its standard profits, it will have to its credit 20 per cent of the excess over 116-6.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the
minister could put on the record something such as I have here from the department, it would be of great value. That is, certain examples of corporations and of individuals. It must be understood that the minister has been talking about corporations, and there has been an increase in the tax on small corporations; or rather the exemption that small corporations had heretofore has been wiped out to a degree if not altogether. Is that not true?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The small corporation has been paying 18 per cent. Hereafter it is proposed that the small corporation shall pay 30 per cent. I might tell the committee the background in my mind of that change. The small corporation, that is the one having less than $5,000 income, before the dominion-provincial agreements, in British Columbia, for example, was paying 28 per cent; that is, 18 per cent to the dominion and 10 per cent

Excess Profits Tax Act
to the province. In Ontario it was paying 23 per cent; that is, 18 per cent to the dominion and 5 per cent to the province; in Quebec, 23 per cent, being 18 per cent to the dominion and 5 per cent to the province. Then we entered into the agreements, and we wiped out the provincial corporation tax on the income of 1941 and did not put on any tax in its place. Therefore the small corporation last year had a favoured position as compared with the position it enjoyed in the past.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: However, the amount of money involved would not be very large.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I do not know; I did not make a computation. But it becomes a matter of judgment as to what tax should be imposed on the small corporation. On the one hand it is in competition with the proprietorship which pays an excess profits tax of 15 per cent; that is the minimum for the proprietorship. On the other hand it is in competition with the corporation which earns a little more than $5,000, to which corporation the rates I have been talking about apply, a minimum of 40 per cent. It is anybody's judgment whether the rate on the small corporation should be 25 per cent or 30 per cent or any intermediate figure or any figure near there. I do not see why 30 per cent is not as near a just tax on the small corporation as anything else. They may think they are unjustly taxed as compared with the unincorporated company, but they enjoy certain advantages in being incorporated, and also they are advantageously treated as compared with the slightly larger company which pays a minimum of 40 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister means they have been advantageously treated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; they will be in the future, because a company having more than $5,000 profits is taxable at a minimum of 40 per cent now, and under the new legislation there has been no change in that 40 per cent minimum. But the company with $5,000 profit or less will pay a minimum of 30 per cent. There is nothing about 40 per cent in regard to that company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suggest to the minister that he put these examples on record They would be valuable to hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have not looked at them. I understand the commissioner of income tax let the hon. gentleman have a memorandum.
44561-260i
I have not seen that memorandum myself. I should like to look at it before I put it on record, although I have no doubt it is correct.

The minister stated in regard to the returnable portion of the excess profits tax, that it referred to only 20 per cent above a certain amount. Is it 20 per cent above the normal 18 per cent, or 20 per cent of wdiat?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is 20 per cent of the amount of profits over and above 116-6 per cent of the standard profits.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like the minister to clarify the position with regard to the second part of this proposal of resolution 4, which he evidently overlooked, that is to say the principle upon which the refundable part is to be repaid. If one looks at resolution 5, it will be observed that a very long delay is going to take place between the payment and the return. For instance, the refundable portion of the tax in respect of the profits of the present year is to be paid not later than the end of the second fiscal period of the government commencing after the cessation of hostilities. I suggest that might be two years after the cessation of hostilities, depending of course on when the proclamation is made. Suppose the proclamation came next March, it is possible this money might be with the government for nearly three years without any interest. I was going to suggest that perhaps that is too _ long, or to ask why the delay of two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It may be repaid before
that, but it may be retained until that time. It may be that conditions during the first year and perhaps part of the second year after the termination of hostilities will be such that the expenditure of money in the country would in the opinion of the government be economically injurious-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The government will not have the money to pay it. That is w-hat the minister is saying?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I did not have that in
mind, but perhaps that is true.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think
that would be the only reason why repayment would be withheld.
* Mr. ILSLEY:	No; after the last war the
armistice was in November, 1918, and it was in 1919 and the spring of 1920 that the most inflationary period of all came. It might be foolish for the government to turn loose more money in a period like that. It would, I think, have been advantageous after the last
Excess Profits Tax Act

war to retain any such money as this until late in 1920 or thereabouts, or 1921, instead of paying it back in 1918 or 1919.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
On the
other hand, if industries are going to turn from war activity to peace-time activity and they have to change their machinery and undertake rehabilitation, they will want to begin as soon as war orders cease. With what funds are they going to do this? These refundable tax payments are not assignable to a bank as security. A company cannot borrow on the strength of them. However, I would assume that any responsible government, upon appropriate representation being made that the situation was one in which the money ought to be repaid, would not unduly withhold the return of this 20 per cent. It is going to be a very important feature in rehabilitation. As the minister has stated, this two-year period is the maximum period that the government can withhold this money. I am sorry -we have not had a little more clarification of the whole position. I think I understand it, though I am not sure I do, but I am not going to delay the committee further. If other hon. members do not think they understand it, they can ask questions.
Mr. O'BRIEN: A few moments ago the leader of the opposition used me in a figure of speech as a horrible example, and it was rather an experience to find myself travelling heavenward. Now, however, since reincarnation has set in, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister my feeling that in this excess profits division there should be a difference in the treatment given two classes of industry to-day. For instance, there is the large business which has been developed purely as a result of the war; in most instances with government capital; certainly with all business coming from the government. In these instances the government furnishes the orders, the cash to pay for them, the inspectors, the capital required to set up the plant, in some-instances perhaps the money required to process the material. In addition, the material is furnished. Of course these companies are doing excellent work in the war effort; but, after all, their position is relatively simple. I am thinking of the primary producer, what I might describe as the owner-manager type of business, such as lumbering, fishing and presumably farming, though farming is not usually called a business.

You need more brains in that than in anything else.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Quite so. People engaged in business of that kind are entirely on their own. Not only do they have to supply their own
IMr. Ilsley.j
capital, but they have to face all the hazards of obtaining their raw material. Those hazards, of course, are provided by the elements. I can imagine a large company, let us say with a pre-war turn-over of perhaps 85,000,000, taking a 10 per cent profit. But that business has been so blown up as a result of the war- and of course it is now exclusively war business that is being done-that the $5,000,000 turn-over has possibly become a $100,000,000 turn-over, so that the 25 per cent they were allowed to retain under the budget of last year is in itself an enormous income, because of the way in which the volume of business has been increased. Every time an order passes through the office of that large corporation, 25 per cent of the profit is retained, and this adds up to an enormous total. On the other hand, in another business the volume may have increased only moderately, and next year that business may suffer a very severe loss. So I maintain that smaller business should be given * a more liberal share of the profits as a protection against the unknown dangers ahead.
Some days ago, I think when delivering his budget speech, the minister said that Canada's war effort had now reached the point where it was not necessary to take capital from profits. That I can quite well understand in connection with the large corporations to which I have referred, but it does not apply to businesses of the other smaller class. In connection with these small companies it is possible that debts incurred during the depression are now being liquidated; yet a small business may want to improve its position, perhaps by putting in a new machine. The only possible source from which money can be secured to put in that machine is profits. These people cannot go to the public and ask for financing, nor are they in a position to come to the government and request capital assistance. So if business of this kind is to continue during the war, not to mention conditions post-war, it is essential that it be given more consideration than is given these large corporations, which, after all, are virtually a branch of government today. The small fellow is simply going along, fighting the hazards on his own responsibility, using his own capital and depending upon his own ingenuity. I believe a system such as I suggest is in operation in the United States, and I would strongly recommend to the minister that if small business is to be developed in this country for the benefit of the war effort, and to meet post-war conditions, this should be done.
Perhaps I might refer briefly to the $500 limit that may be left in any business, which of course comes under the succession duties division. It was in this connection that the

Excess Profits Tax Act
leader of the opposition referred to my particular case. Of course when I die and daisies begin growing over me it really does not make very much difference to me what happens to my estate, or to anyone else except those men whom I am to-day employing. I am only a symbol in the social order to-day; because I have position, and all that sort of thing, I am able to pass on to others the advantages to which they are entitled. There is a theory abroad in this land that the world owes a man a living. It does not; but it distinctly owes him a chance to earn a living, and if capital is going to be taken away in this manner, the person from whom the money is taken is not injured, but those left behind, facing responsibilities with which they are not able to cope, are the ones who are going to suffer.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the situation with regard to one industry, that of ranching, which might well be described as a depressed industry. During the standard years conditions were very bad for those engaged in ranching, so that instead of having any profits at all, they suffered losses. During the last year or so conditions have been somewhat better, but the ranchers are all in debt, and now they will have 100 per cent of their profits taken away, since all their profits will be excess profits because, based on the standard years, they had no profits at all. Is there any likelihood of the board of referees considering such cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The board of referees under the Excess Profits Tax Act is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue, who might have some knowledge of what action if any has been taken in reference to the ranchers of Alberta. I know that when I was in the west a year ago a delegation came to see me, making representations that the ranching industry should be classified as a depressed industry within the meaning of the Excess Profits Tax Act, but I do not know what happened afterwards. There is abundant machinery for dealing with cases of that kind. I assume that they have applied to the board of referees in the usual course and have received the fair and just treatment which business men tell me is the treatment they receive from that board.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wanted to ask something in that connection also. There is no doubt that the setting up of this board has served a useful purpose. I think it is the accepted opinion that it was a very high-class board, that they had skilful and competent auditors and advisers who prepared the
docket for them in each case and that once they got into their stride they were able to handle a great many cases quickly. On the assumption that a company was in the depressed industry class, that it was a company that had no standard profits, then the board of referees would have the case referred to it by the minister. I understand that, must be done under the law, that a case does: not go to the board automatically but must be referred to it by the minister, and that' the board deals with a man's case on the1 basis of the examination that has been made1 of his position. If he comes within the category of a depressed industry, then under the law he is allowed a return of so much per cent on the capital investment. Is that a correct statement to make?
Mr, ILSLEY: That is right.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On that basis, when he begins to earn sufficient to come under the Excess Profits Tax Act, he then pays the ordinary corporation income tax; he pays that in addition to the excess profits tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes, if he has had excess profits.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He has a different base. One company which is not in the depressed industry class has a historical base, and the other has a base which is computed by the board. Whatever is earned is then subject to the ordinary operation of the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

What reason has the minister for not paying interest on the returnable portion? The government is making full use of this with intention that it shall go back to< the industry, and I think it would be a reasonable thing to pay interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The first intention of the government was to treat this returnable portion as being something less than the property of the company. I believe they did this for a while in Great Britain. However, after consideration we thought that we should regard it as the company's money to be refunded, but we did not take the final step of making interest payable on it. There is nee particular rule which would indicate that we should. When I say that our first intention was to treat it as being something less than the company's money we had in mind providing that the company should put it to a certain use, otherwise they would not have it back.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The government held a string on it?
Excess Pro fils T ax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member for Rosetown-Bigga, (Mr. Coldwell) argued most forcibly that that is exactly what we ought to do, but there were many difficulties in the way. To begin with, a condition which the government might feel justified in attaching to the return of the money could be that it be used to furnish employment or be invested in capital investments. That would be impossible for a large number of companies. There are commercial enterprises, insurance companies, and other companies of that type which could not invest money in any employmentgiving asset. We thought there would be serious discrimination arising between different types of companies.
To a certain extent we were guided by the experience of Great Britain. I have not a thorough knowledge of their law, but my impression is that the first year the British government levied a tax of 100 per cent on excess profits, they agreed to return 20 per cent. The agreement had certain elements of vagueness about it, and the result was that the companies did not consider the 20 per cent as an asset. The British government found that the incentive to economy and efficiency in management and operation was lacking because from the companies' point of view the whole 100 per cent excess was gone. Why be economical, why try if the whole thing is gone? The government then began to move toward the companies, so to speak. Either the second or the third year, I am not sure of my dates, but certainly this year the British government made it clear that the money was the companies' money. I assume they did so because they felt it was necessary to agree to that in order to provide some incentive for economy and the cutting down of expenses and the running of business as business ought to be run.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They
created a credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They created a credit. There was no mistake as to whose money it was. It was money refundable to the companies, and that provided some incentive to carry on in the usual prudent and economical way in which business enterprises conduct their affairs. For one reason or another we felt that if we were to preserve that incentive in this country we should do that. We decided to do it as a matter of policy rather than to rely entirely upon a desire to do the right thing or a willingness to do the right thing on the part of all companies. We felt that we would have to make it clear that this money was the company's money and that this credit would be returned within the period
IMr. R. B. Hanson.]
provided, but we did not feel any obligation to go farther and pay interest. The government had every right to take 100 per cent and keep it if they wished to, to take it as a tax, but we decided as a matter of policy, to take the course we have followed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Interest is paid on the compulsory saving portion of the personal income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are treating the individual better than the corporation, and there is an excellent reason for that. The money that we get from the individual is not excess profits. It must be remembered that the money we are taking from these companies is excess profits presumably made out of the war and, morally, the government has every right to take all of it and keep it.
Not all of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Any excess.

The difference between 18 and 40 per cent is not money made out of the war. That is how I characterized the so-called excess profits tax when it was imposed two years ago. It is an excess tax on profits in connection with a substantial part of it. Any company which is earning the same amount as it did prior to the war is taxed 40 per cent rather than 18 per cent because of the imposition of the excess profits tax. If it is earning less than it earned in the pre-war years, it is still taxed 40 per cent. This is the only type of activity in the country that is taxed in this manner; farming and other forms of activity are not taxed unless they are in a corporate form. I think we should be fair about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I went too far in saying that the government is morally entitled to the whole excess. Opinions differ as to what the government has a moral right to do, but I think it has a moral right to appropriate that part which is war profits. There could be no exception taken even by the most enthusiastic upholder of private initiative to that point of view. It was not on moral grounds that we provided for the return of the 20 per cent; it was on the ground of meeting an expediency and providing an incentive. We felt that we would get a much better result, but we did not feel there was an obligation to pay interest.
When we came to the individual we were not necessarily taking his money out of excess earnings. In most instances we were not. We are providing that if they have certain kinds of savings we will accept those in lieu of the payments made to us. They will

Excess Profits Tax Act
get interest on these other savings, or something equivalent to interest, and therefore it is appropriate to allow the short term rate of interest.

The returnable portion of
the excess profits tax is a corporation or company asset, which, however, for the duration of the war and a period thereafter is frozen. In the event of a company having to go into bankruptcy or liquidation, is there any process by which that returnable portion can be returned to. the company in order to help liquidate or wind up the estate? Emergencies may arise necessitating the quick winding up of an estate, and yet the company may have this asset which is in the hands of the government. Can these companies get anything to indicate that they have an asset of this kind, and is it transferable or negotiable, or is there any process by which under special circumstances it can be returned at an earlier date than indicated in the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was considered when
the resolution and the legislation were being prepared, but we felt that the liquidator would just have to wait. It is not an unusual thing for liquidators to wait, sometimes for years, but we hope it will not be for many years. There is no provision for paying that money out to bankrupt companies any earlier than we pay it out to solvent companies. It cannot be paid out under this legislation until after the cessation of hostilities, and I do not think we would be justified in providing that if a company went into bankruptcy it could get the money any earlier.
Suppose that death necessitates the winding up of a solvent company. Is there any process by which the returnable portion could be turned over to the estate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on this subject, but I have been waiting until we reach resolution 5, which I think would be the appropriate one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would suggest to the committee that resolutions 1 to 5 be taken together because they are interlocking. If that be agreeable to the committee, we shall proceed accordingly.

Agreed.
2.	That in computing the amount of excess profits subject to the tax of 100 per centum, corporations be allowed to deduct such portion of the income tax and the tax payable under the third part of the second schedule to the excess Profits Tax Act as the excess profits bear to the total profits.
3.	That the exemption from excess profits tax of. corporations with profits not in excess
of $5,000 be limited to an exemption from the tax under the first part or the second part of the second schedule but that such corporations be subject to the tax under the third part of the second schedule, namely, a tax, of 12 per centum of profits.
4.	That there shall be refunded to the taxpayer in accordance with paragraph five of these resolutions an amount equal to 20 per centum of the profits above the point at which the tax calculated under the first part of the second schedule is equal to the tax calculated under the second part of the second schedule, provided that the said profits have been paid by way of taxes under the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, to the Receiver General of Canada.
5.	That the refundable portion of any tax exigible under any enactment founded on these resolutions shall be repaid to the taxpayer or to his legal representatives, after the cessation of hostilities between Canada and Germany, Italy and Japan, and in the following manner: The refundable portion of the tax in respect of the profits of 1942 and fiscal periods ending therein, shall be repaid at such times and in such instalments as the governor in council may determine but not later than the end of the second fiscal period of the government commencing after the said cessation of hostilities; the refundable portion of the tax in respect of the profits of 1943 and fiscal periods ending therein shall be repaid at such times and in such instalments as the governor in council may determine but not later than the end of the third fiscal year of the government commencing after the said cessation of hostilities and so on in resjrect of the refundable portion of the tax on the profits of successive years or fiscal periods.
The date of the cessation of hostilities shall be deemed to be the date of a proclamation issued under the authority of the governor in council declaring that, for purposes of the said refund, the war no longer exists.

I was very sorry to hear the minister say a few moments ago that the point which I had raised in the budget debate, had been carefully considered but had been more or less discarded for the time being. As a matter of fact I have drafted an amendment to resolution 5 which I intend to put forward to test the feeling of the committee, and I hope yet that the minister will reconsider this question. After all, we are dealing, not with profits but with excess profits. These excess profits are being made largely out of the distress of the nation, and to my mind they ought never to be considered as an asset of a company, corporation or individual. They ought to be the property of the people of Canada out of whose distress these profits are being made. Therefore I think we should take 100 per cent of all excess profits over and above the base allowed, but the government has decided otherwise.
The minister said a few minutes ago that one of the considerations which had governed in the decision of the department was that it was very' difficult to differentiate between what
Excess Profits Tax Act

I might term an industrial corporation operating an industry and a commercial one, such as an insurance company or something of that sort. If we are going to return any part of the excess profits-and the minister proposes under this to return 20 per cent-the only justification for returning any part would be that the profit was to be used for the rehabilitation of the industry in its transition from war-time to peace-time activity, or for the creation of employment during a consequent period of unemployment or during the demobilization period, or to bring some good of some sort to the people of Canada. I would suggest that a commercial organization like an insurance company is not required to rehabilitate itself in the post-war period in the same way as an industrial company, and1 therefore that consideration should not enter into the decision at all. If such companies make an excess profit, we should take 100 per cent of that excess profit.
I read an article in this morning's Montreal Gazette with which I thoroughly agree. It was by Professor Harold Laski, of London. Professor Laski pointed out that we are losing this war to-day because we insist on maintaining a system which makes it impossible for us to conduct this war in the same manner in which our opponents are conducting their war, and the result is that our compromises bring chaos and inefficiency.
I wanted to move something which I thought would be acceptable, and I am going to place it before the committee now so that when we come to resolution 5 it will receive more consideration than it has received up to the present time. My suggestion is this:
That section 5 be amended by the insertion of the words "under such conditions" after the word "times" in the sixth line of the section, and by insertion of the same words "under such conditions" after the word "times" in the tenth line of the section.
Further, that after the word "periods" at the end of the first paragraph, the following words be added:
"Provided, however, that all such refundable portions of the tax in respect of the profits aforementioned, shall not be used for the payment of dividends, bonuses, or otherwise disbursed except for the rehabilitation of the industry, the provision of employment or such other service to the Canadian people as the governor in council may determine."
I am going to pass that to the Chairman so that the amendment may be considered when we reach the appropriate clause. I think it is altogether wrong for us to leave any loophole whatsoever which will allow at the conclusion of the war any corporation or company to defeat the very objective of the excess profits tax and to use the accumulated refundable portion of the tax for dividends 
and bonuses to their shareholders. I say that no one has the right to make a profit out of the blood and agony of the people of this country in this war, and it is our duty to see to it that nothing of that sort is done now or in the future.
I want to be quite clear about what I have in mind. First of all I do not think any portion of the excess profits tax should be refunded, but since it has been decided to refund 20 per cent, then I would say that if it is to be refunded it should be refunded to be used as the governor in council may determine, for the creation of work or for the transition of industry from war-time to peacetime activity. In other words, we should not regard the refundable excess profits as the property of a company or corporation to do with as they wish, but as a common gift to all the people of Canada to help rehabilitate some of the industrial life of this nation after the war is over. I again urge the minister to give consideration to the point of view I have suggested.

I wish to tell the committee a homely story which was given me the other day, and which I think has value and has a bearing on the point raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Out at the western coast the owner of a fishing boat came into a marine depot at the height of a very good fishing season. The owner of the depot asked him if he wished to fill up his tank with oil, and the proprietor of the boat said, "No, I just came in to return an article which I borrowed the other day." "Well", the owner of the marine depot said, "I am very much surprised that that is the case, that you are not filling up. Surely you are not laying up your boat at the height of a good fishing season?" The owner of the boat said, "Yes, that is just what I am doing. I have had a very good season so far, an excellent season. If I take the boat out again I run a certain risk of losing it, and if I make any more money the government will take whatever I earn, and I have decided that my wisest course is to lay up the boat and go down to the prairies and make a visit to some friends which I intended making."
As I say, that is a homely story, but it has an important lesson for us who are attempting to improve methods of taxation and at the same time raise the moneys which necessarily must be raised for our war effort. I have always thought that, while nobody would care to argue against the proposition-it is the natural desire of every hon. member-that no person shall make any profit out of the suffering of the people as a result of the war effort,

Excess Profits Tax Act
we must keep in mind that there must be the incentive to the whole of the people of Canada to produce annually just as much goods and services as is humanly possible. If we remove the natural incentive to produce other than the minimum, we destroy any hope of producing the maximum. I for one would suggest to the Minister of Finance that he see to it that the fact that 20 per cent is taken and kept as a saving for the individual is made well known to the people of Canada, and that a special campaign of advertising is used for that purpose. In the ordinary corporation with legal or accounting advice there will be no misinterpretation of this particular provision in regard to the 20 per cent; but the great majority of individuals is rather of the opinion that when the government takes money without giving in return a bond or some other formal acknowledgment, it intends never to give it back, and the promise contained in a statute which most people do not read leaves them in the unfortunate position of not recognizing that this section does supply the incentive I spoke about, and that by continuing to produce fish, or whatever it may be their task to produce, they add to the annual wealth from which we can take these taxes. I suggest it will be wise economy for the minister to attempt to bring home to the people of Canada that it is both patriotic and profitable to work as hard and produce as much as possible during this war period.

Would the minister explain to the committee how he has arrived at the conclusion that you must give a corporation or a company a certain amount of excess profits tax as an incentive to produce, but you can expect the hundreds of thousands of people, the workers, who actually do the production, to produce without any incentive as far as this particular budget is concerned? I fail to see in it any provision where any individual worker is given any incentive to produce. His wages are frozen; his income tax is increased; he apparently needs no incentive. Yet production, in the final analysis, depends upon the multitude of workers as much as it does upon the industrial corporation oi company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The ordinary run of mankind does require an incentive, even in time of war, to produce. We have delegations repeatedly from farmers and others who say they cannot be expected to produce farm products unless the price is sufficient to give them some incentive, and we are blamed for not arranging matters so that the price does give them that incentive. We hear in this chamber hon. members who say that if we desire greater
production it is a simple thing to get it by increasing the price. For instance, I have heard the hon. member for Lethbridge say that if we were to make the price of farm products high enough we need not worry about getting the farm products.
With regard to labour I am a little bit out of the field. The Minister of Labour would be much better to expound this matter than I am. But I do not think we would get men to work overtime unless we paid them the wages for working overtime. There are some men who work overtime on the ordinary day rate, but I think most workers require time and a half, or in some cases double time, in order to work overtime. That is what I mean by incentive; and they would not work without the incentive, or a great many of them certainly would not.
Then, I under-stand, there are reclassifications and promotions in industry. An apprentice goes in at a certain wage. If he qualifies himself for a better position, a higher classification, he gets that higher classification. But he does not do the work in the higher classification unless he gets a higher wage. The higher wage he is to get is the incentive which induces him to qualify himself for the higher-range. of duties, and he gets it. That is a profit, for under our laws that is not denied by any order in council or any law that I know of. Indeed, promotions and reclassifications of labour in industry are continually taking place. We are told that unless we want to disorganize the whole productive machinery of the country we must give labour some monetary incentive. The labourer is given it, and he responds to it.
I wish we did not have to do that. I wish that everybody would, in a time like this, work as a great many do, apparently, without any incentive at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Service to the state ought to be a good incentive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know there are executives, boards of directors of companies, and others who, if I am any judge, do not require a monetary incentive to do everything they possibly can, because they believe everything is at stake. Then there are others who have not attained that high state of sacrifice, or perhaps comprehension, and they say, "Well, what is the use? Am I going to run the risk of a loss if, when I make a profit, it is all taken away from me?" That is the way some talk. I did not make people that way. If I were constructing them perhaps I would construct them in a different way, but that is the way they are. It is not confined to business. It is not confined to big corporations. You will find it, I fancy, among
Excess Profits Tax Act

members of this house. You find it among all classes and all callings, high and low, rich and poor. It is what might properly be called human nature. I think that answers the hon. gentleman.

I would ask the
minister to observe that we have been talking about excess profits, and I fail to see where workers in any classification are likely to get much in the way of excess profits as an incentive to produce. I am glad to hear the minister say that consideration has been given to the incentive motive as far as the worker, the actual producer, is concerned. You will find in the budget later that there are points in it which suggest that the worker would be just as well off if he did not work overtime. I have had a number of instances of that called to my attention which will come up in another connection. But as to the question of getting excess profits as an incentive to produce, I do not think the minister is consistent in his dealings with the companies as compared with his dealings with individuals as workers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me say something about" these excess profits which it is assumed it will be possible for companies to earn. If a company makes any excess profits whatever; if it makes 100 per cent of its pre-war earnings-exactly 100 per cent-it will be permitted under this taxation to retain 60 per cent. If it makes 116-6 per cent, it will be permitted to retain 70 per cent. If it makes 150 per cent of its pre-war earnings, it will be permitted to retain 76-7 per cent. If it makes 200. per cent of its pre-war earnings, it will be permitted to retain 86-7 per cent. If it makes 250 per cent of its pre-war earnings, it will be permitted to retain 96-7 per cent. If it- makes 300 per cent of its pre-war earnings, it will be permitted to retain 10&-7 per cent-and when I say retain, I am including the 20 per cent refundable. No company can retain more than 70 per cent of its pre-war earnings leaving out that 20 per cent refundable, so that I have tried to make this taxation such that my hon. friend and his associates will not need to worry about the amount that will be left in the hands of the companies. The figures I have given are rather significant.
It is a great improvement.

I do not think the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) with regard to agriculture should be allowed to pass unchallenged. He has said that agriculture has asked for a price that will give some incentive, and he referred to statements

made by the hon. member for Lethbridge. The hon. member for Lethbridge has never asked that the farmer should be allowed prices which would return excess profits. All he has asked for is that the farmer shall receive a parity price which will return to him his cost of production; in other words, a price which is commensurate with the price that he has to pay for other commodities. Unless the farmer receives that price, he cannot pay his costs and he is bound to go into debt. To try to draw a comparison between that situation and the situation where the manufacturers want to have refunded to them excess profits is certainly not very fair. The farmers are not even asking for a price that will return a fair profit; as I say, they are simply asking for a parity price that will make it possible for them to pay cost of production. I do not think the minister made a sound argument when he tried to compare agriculture with other industries which made substantial profits before the war and which are now making handsome excess profits.

I am prompted to say a
few words on this matter because of remarks made by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham). I know him to be a pretty solid person, and I was surprised at the homely story he told the committee in order to protect those who require excess profits. Evidently he believes in profitable patriotism; if you do not get well paid for fighting the war, you should not fight it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has made our position clear with the amendment with respect to excess profits. The industrialists to-day are doing a job to save their own skins as well as those of the rest of the nation, and they are guaranteed pre-war profits.
Oh no; how do you make that out?

Oh, yes. The normal profits of the last three years are taken as the base, and it is computed from that. If we had facilities at our disposal to probe thoroughly the excess profits question, it would startle some of us. I am not satisfied that the figures we have been getting are correct. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) may have reason to think they are, but we are not satisfied. The hon. member for Swift Current makes certain statements with regard to fishermen, and I am doubtful whether there are any fishermen in Canada who would take the attitude suggested by that hon. gentleman. I do not think there is any fisherman who would use 25 per cent of the fishing season to make sufficient money to care for his own
Excess Profits Tax Act
needs and then, because of taxation, decline to produce any more, taking a vacation to visit his friends, and contributing nothing to the treasury. Any man who takes that attitude at a time like this should be interned, because he is definitely no asset to the nation. What would the hon. member for Swift Current think of the average industrial worker employed six .days a week who took certain time off for similar reasons? He does not wish to work overtime, but in the majority of cases he is forced to do so by circumstances.
It is not because he wants to do so. By working six days a week the great majority of them bring themselves within the range of the income tax. The great majority of them contribute the last two days they work by way of taxation. What would the hon. member think if each week they worked for four days and then stayed at home for two days, taking care of their recreational requirements, looking after their health, going on a fishing trip, and so on. What would he think of them if they took that attitude and argued that because they worked two additional days a wreek they would be contributing to the treasury by way of taxation. He would call them saboteurs, and rightly so. But the industrialist or manufacturer who takes advantage of the war situation to put a gun to the head of the Minister of Finance or anyone else in the country charged with the responsibility of directing that particular phase of our war effort is just as much a saboteur as those who would spend two days a week at home instead of producing because, by producing, they would come within the scope of the income tax. There is no difference. I would advise the hon. member to advise his friend who refused to fish because he might have to pay tax that if he is visiting in Saskatchewan now he should take that boat out and be a Canadian citizen and1 make his contribution.
I rose to say that because the position is absolutely analogous. I have a document showing the contribution some industrial workers are making by way of taxation a large percentage of what they get. What is shown as paid directly is a very small proportion of their tax, direct and indirect, but they are not doing any squawking about it.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in his remarks and the amendment proposed has made the position clear; there should be no excess profits; no one should make any money out of this war. Our attitude should be that of New Zealand, that no one shall be any richer because he has not gone to the war, that no one who has gone to the war shall be any worse off when he comes back because he went to the war and made his
contribution. If that 20 per cent of the excess profits tax is not used in rehabilitation after the war, then I say that those who are charged with the responsibility and have the authority of legislating are failing in their duty to those who have offered their all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the hon. member consider that excess profits and war profits are synonymous? I think there is a distinction. One may include part of the other, but they are not synonymous.
No, they are not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then the hon. member must make a distinction between the two.
I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Acadia said. I was surprised when the minister spoke of the farmer as *wanting excess profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said nothing of the kind.
That was the implication.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it was not. There was no such implication. The hon. gentleman was asking me why people needed incentives, and I was explaining that every normal person wants incentives. I was not blaming the farmer.
Put it this way; the incentive the minister was talking about was the incentive of making a profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.
Excess profits.

Well, the minister says no. I accept his word. The reason why there have been so many delegations of farmers waiting on the government during recent years was not that the farmers were asking for a profit, but that they were asking for a price which would be more nearly commensurate with the cost of production, which they were not getting at that time. Let us not get these things mixed up.
They want a profit over the cost of production.

They were not asking for a profit over the cost of production; the figures we have produced from time to time amply show that over a period of years they were not getting cost of production when they were getting 70 cents or even 90 cents a bushel for wheat at Fort William. As long as men and women are able to see life now and security in the future, that is what they ask as a rule. The bulk of our population
Excess Profits Tax Act

never see that at all. We are not discussing that; we are discussing the question of excess profit, and, as I said earlier, if I had my way at this time-and this would be a compromise-I would take 100 per cent of all profit over, say a base profit of 4 per cent.
Would the hon. member take that from the farmer too?

The farmer does not get 4 per cent. If he got 4 per cent in addition to the cost of production year in and year out, he would be tickled to death. But let us not get into that. I would take 100 per cent. I say this again, that until we recognize that in this war there ought to be no profit, and get as near as we can to equality of sacrifice in that particular field*-of course there can be no real equality of sacrifice when men are giving their lives-we shall not have the kind of war effort that we ought to have. As I said in quoting the article I read to-day by Harold Laski, we are to-day in the position we are in because we have refused to recognize that this is not a war in the sense we have talked about war in the past; it is in effect a world revolution; it is in effect the demand of the plain ordinary man for the right to live decently apart from monopolies and with no one making a profit out of his production and labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That is what Hitler
says.

We should take all
profits above a minimum amount.

I am glad to hear this discussion on the general principle of the excess profits tax, because I would call into question the fundamentals of this legislation. It is arbitrary in its arrangement; it is based on no sound principle. The excess is what a manufacturer or business man makes over and above what he made in some standard period. What he made in the standard period may itself have been excess.

Or less.
i

Or on the contrary it may have been below what is a normal profit. So the excess profits tax is geared up to allow perhaps more than normal profits to those who were in business and doing well during the standard period, and with almost diabolical ingenuity to exempt from extreme taxation those concerns which are well established as against those which were not doing business, or were making very small profits, or no profits, during the standard period. The great gold mining companies were doing very well during the standard period.
They saved the country during the great depression.

They did very well, they and their employees, in producing gold which helped our exchange position. I am not attacking them. We are now talking about what is fair as between various classes of producers. The gold mining companies were making big money during the standard period, and what they then made is the standard now of normal profits to that industry. It is only profits in excess of the great profits they made in those years that are now considered excess profits.. The financial institutions, the thoroughly established ones, were doing well during that period. So were the manufac-. turers-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not all.

Not all, but the big
standard ones were doing well. The fact that some were not doing well does not answer my criticism of the general principle of this taxation.
I submit there is something to be said in favour of the principle laid down by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation; that is, that all companies should be treated alike and that whatever your rate of normal tax may be, it should be applied to all, big and small, those who were making profits previously and those who were not. I do not say 4 per cent is sufficient; I do not know, but it would be fairer were we to allow profit at some standard rate upon the investment of the company and call all profits above that rate excess profits.
Would you guarantee the profits of those companies that did not make any?

I do not think the question is asked seriously. Of course you will not guarantee profits; if you do you keep in existence unprofitable businesses, which would be a loss to the country. That has been a principle of the Conservative party throughout the ages, to bolster those concerns which did not make a natural, normal profit, to give them, by tariffs and other favours, profits which they could not otherwise make, and to charge the losses up to the paying business of the country. That is abnormal; that is not sound, and I do not believe in it. A business that cannot make profits should close its doors.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I suppose the Liberal party never did anything like that.?

Why are you trying to bring party politics into this discussion? At all events, the Conservative party has no

reason to complain about the tariff measures of the Liberal party, which have always been very much more moderate than when hon. gentlemen opposite have been in office.
Are you sure?
I am perfectly satisfied as to that. But that sort of talk is a red herring across this trail.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Who
started it?
You started it. I was trying to discuss the principles underlying the excess profits tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And you levelled a charge against the Conservative party.
Well, if I have made any charges against the poor Conservative party I withdraw them. It is in a bad fix now, and I do not want to do it any more damage than has been done.
Oh, oh.
There will be a chance for all of you to make speeches when I get through.
I doubt it.

Well, you have made a good many more than I have so far. A good deal of the time of the house is consumed in chit-chat from across the way. Now let me get back to what I was saying, because I was trying to make a point clear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So important you cannot remember.

please not interrupt?

I endorse the general principles, though not the exact amount, stated by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. I think there is something sound in the principle he has enunciated, that all companies should pay the same; that all companies should be allowed the same rate of normal profits, and that everything in excess of that rate should be considered excess profit. During war time I have no objection to taking all truly excess profits and not paying back anything.
