speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before
resolution 5 is carried I want to ask the minister a question with respect to the words "cessation of hostilities". Is the committee to understand that the cessation of hostilities referred to there is to be a special date for the purposes of the refund, or will it be the official date of the cessation of hostilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not intended that it shall be selected for the purpose of determining the date of the refund.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is what I am asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only reason for providing that it shall be fixed by the governor in council is that the date of the cessation of hostilities may be difficult to ascertain as a matter .of fact. It is impossible to foresee what the condition of affairs will be. Some nations may be fighting on; there may be none fighting; the fighting may stop and then start again. One can hardly tell what sort of world we shall be living in; we are using a term in this measure which is not susceptible of exact determination by evidence, and therefore it must be fixed by the governor in council. I think wherever terms such as "the end of the war" or "the cessation of hostilities" are used in legislation there is always some means provided for making an exact determination of that date. I know under the War Measures Act a proclamation is provided for.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is the proclamation which I assumed to be applicable in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That proclamation may not be accurate; the War Measures Act may run for a period after the termination of the war, as it did before.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Did it run after the proclamation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but the war ceased, I would say, on the date of the armistice in November, 1918. The War Measures Act, however, did not pass out until 1919 or 1920.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The armistice was only the cessation of actual fighting; there was a long period in between the armistice and the latter stages, so the war was not over officially until the peace treaty was signed.
Excess Profits Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether it was over then, but that is the very point. I would have said the armistice was the date, but my hon. friend thinks it was the date of the peace treaty. Maybe neither was the actual date of the cessation of hostilities; and because that is an ambiguous term provision is made for fixing the date by order in council.

But you do not intend to have any date fixed for the purposes of this question of refund? That is not going to be fixed having regard only to that feature; the general date of the cessation of hostilities or of the peace will be the date contemplated here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, the members of the group of which I am a member intend to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. We feel as he does with regard to the matter of excess profits. These excess profits-and I am sorry to say that I believe the minister confused them with ordinary profits-as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said are obtained as a consequence of the agony of the people of this country. We feel that the 20 per cent which is returnable should be returnable only with the clear-cut understanding that, as the amendment sets out, it is to be used during the transition period, when industries now producing materials of war will revert to the production of peace-time consumer goods. To the extent that this 20 per cent is used for that purpose we would have no objection to its refund, or to the extent that it might be used to assist in the estblishment of workers who of necessity will lose positions in war industries and must be given positions in the peace-time industrial life of this country. Many of the boys who are now overseas fighting will come back to this country maimed, and will find that they have to fight for all they are worth to secure a mere pittance as a pension. We do not feel that there is anything in the way of excess profits being paid to them after the war, and therefore we are of the opinion that the industries have no claim upon excess profits which may be used, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said, to pay dividends to shareholders. We are in favour of the amendment and intend to support it.

I am going to support this amendment. The hon. member for Rosetown-
(Mr R. B. Hanson.]
Biggar has put the case very well. This returnable portion of the tax should not be used by the companies to pay dividends; it should be used to provide employment. So far as farmers are concerned, I think the money should be used for rehabilitation purposes and improvements. I do not agree with the hon. member for Northumberland, New Brunswick (Mr. O'Brien) who said that farmers are not business men. I say it requires more brains to make a success of farming than it does to make a success of any other industry.
Mr. O'BRIEN: I meant that farming is generally carried on by the individual and does not provide the same form of employment as industry. Of course, the larger the farming operation, the more like a business it becomes.

I think it is agreed that the agricultural industry requires brains to make a success of it. It has been said that no one should be better off after this war. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) has said that the agricultural industry has been a depressed industry, not only since the war but for many years before. This industry provides more new wealth than any other industry in Canada. There are many farms in western Canada where new machinery and improvements are needed, and if any farmers are in a position where 20 per cent will be returned, I think it should be used for that purpose. I am going to support this amendment. As the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) says, the farmers have not been unreasonable or have not asked for too much. All they have been asking for is parity so far as production costs are concerned. They have been producing at less than cost without complaining too much.

' I think it should be said at this time that the farm delegations which came here were not asking for profits. The average cost of producing a bushel of wheat in the west before the war was $1, and all the farmer is getting is 70 cents a bushel at the farm. The farmers are continuing to grow wheat-they must grow it to live-and yet they must sell it at 30 per cent below the cost of production. They continue to grow wheat because they know it is needed in the winning of this war. The present indications are that they will grow 400,000,000 bushels this year, but they are doing it at a loss. They feel badly when they hear about companies making excess profits. When they know that a discussion is going on as to how those excess profits will be dealt with and what will be done with the portion to be

Excess Profits Tax Act
returned, they will be looking carefully to find out what the House of Commons thinks of this principle. There is a deep and important principle involved. Large profits are being made out of war industries, out of the making of implements of destruction. The armament makers of the world have created wars in the past for the sake of the profits they might make. What do' the members of this House of Commons think should be done with the profits made out of war industry?
A. member who votes for this amendment is voting that such profits shall be used for the reestablishment of the nation, and a member who votes against the amendment is voting in favour of these companies being permitted to make their profits, being permitted to make what I call blood-money.

I should like to say a word in support of this amendment. I was rather surprised at the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) with regard to agriculture. I know many farmers who would have sold out had they not felt that it was patriotic to keep going during the last year or two, even though they were short of help. As I have pointed out before in this house, I do not know how many farmers are going to be able to pay their way and take care of past obligations. Why should we have, on the one hand, a set-up for industry, and expect, on the other hand, the agriculturist to produce at below cost? If industry is to have this 20 per cent which is to be set aside until after the war-
If they earn it.

If they earn it, all right. If it is set aside, it -certainly should be used for rehabilitation purposes. In my part of the country the farmers have been going behind for a number of years, and with the present budget resolutions I do not know how they will be able to take care of past obligations and pay their income taxes, even though they have good crops. They are in a hopeless position. I am going to support this amendment, and I hope the minister will see his way clear to do something for the agriculturists.
Has the minister stated whether the company to whom this 20 per cent is returnable may use it for any purpose they wish?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
It is left open to the companies to use it for any purpose they wish?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is just as though they lent the money to the government without interest.

Surely the minister is riding two horses when he says that. I advanced the opinion a little while ago that since this was the companies' money and the government was making use of it, it should be returned with interest. The minister took the view that excess profits were something it was perfectly proper for the government to take. Then, out of bounty it proposes to return 20 per cent of those profits under certain conditions and at a certain time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say anything about bounty.

Perhaps I am not repeating the minister's words, but he did say the government had decided to return 20 per cent of the tax it is taking, a tax which he says it is perfectly legitimate for the government of Canada to take and retain, but it has now been decided to return 20 per cent of it. It seems to me that it would be reasonable if the government were to take the view that the main purpose for which that returning was done was for the purpose of rehabilitation, to restore industry to that position in which it can make beneficial use of its opportunities by the provision of work for the people. If the government takes the view that it will exercise no guidance whatever with regard to the use to which this money is put by the companies concerned, I must support the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I spoke a few moments ago commending some of the general principles expressed by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party. That is one thing, but it is quite another thing to support this amendment. I am going to vote against it, and I am going to tell you why.
I hope that by the time this war is over wre shall be done with government interference with private business. An attempt on the part of the government, perhaps, years before this money will be repaid, to regulate its expenditures after it is repaid would be the very extreme of governmental interference. Surely, if this money is in the nature of a loan to the government or is not altogether taxes which are to be kept and never returned, the least that we can do is to allow people who receive the money to use it as their best judgment dictates. Their judgment exercised at the time must be better than ours, exercised long in advance and through a government department. I would hesitate to interfere w-ith private busi-
Excess Profits Tax Act

ness in the handling of its own funds after the war is over, perhaps years from now. We have too much government interference now.

I am surprised at the argument made by the hon. member for Trinity. I would be pleased indeed to see excess profits wiped out altogether, and I w'ould like to see my hon. friend introducing an amendment along the lines in which he suggested he was in agreement with me. But I realize that the government has adopted this principle, and therefore what we are trying to do to-night is to see to it that this amount which is to be returned shall not be used by the companies simply as deferred dividends, as post-war bonuses, as melons, if you like, to be cut in the future. In that respect we are trying to safeguard the Canadian people.
I do not agree with the hon. member, of course, when he says that what we should do is to refrain from telling business in the future what it should do. I want to tell him this, that in my opinion the day has gone for good when business can do what it likes. The world will never return to economic anarchy. I once heard an hon. gentleman who sits opposite say to me, "I am an anarchist philosophically and the nearest approach to anarchy that I can find at the present time is the Liberal party". That is fundamentally correct.
On the other hand, we are living in an ordered world, and in my opinion this house, in deciding at this time that we are going to return to industry after the war any portion of its excess profits-and that is the principle which the government has laid down-should also safeguard the nation by seeing that this money shall be used only for the rehabilitation of industry, for the provision of employment, for the good of the nation, and shall not be used simply to pay deferred dividends, bonuses, and so on. I think we should lay down that principle to-night and not wait until some future day when a vested interest will have been acquired in this particular fund.
I am surprised at the argument of the hon. member for Trinity. Someone has said that these industries were not doing any too well to-day. But on June 11 my hon. friend the member for Weyburn put on the record a list of war companies picked at random from the newspapers, and showed that their aggregate profit increase in 1941 over the 1936-39 average was no less than 62 per cent. Take Aluminum Limited, a very prosperous Canadian company in pre-war years. Its average 
profit in the base period, 1936-39, was $9 454,000, and that had increased in 1941 to $16J)15,-000; Consolidated Mining and Smelting increased from an average profit in the 193639 period of $9,294,000 to $12,199,000 in 1941; Ford of Canada increased from $949,000 in the 1936-39 period to $3,379,000 in 1941, and so on.

How much taxes did they
pay in those years?

These were the profits
after the taxes had been paid. It is not a matter of what taxes you pay; it is what you have left after you have paid your taxes that counts. I say that we have a perfect right to make to-night the stipulation the amendment suggests, and not leave it to some future date. I strongly urge the committee to support the amendment I have moved.

7.	That the definition of "standard profits" be amended to exclude therefrom dividends deemed to hare been received under the provisions of section 19 of the Income War Tax Act.

Would the minister
explain just what is meant by that? I have not the Income War Tax Act in front of me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Section 19 of the Income
War Tax Act relates to the winding up of companies and deems undistributed income to have been distributed as a dividend and taxable in that year in the hands of the recipient. It will be obvious that if a receiving company had received such a dividend in the standard' period, it would constitute a very unusual and abnormal profit which should not be allowed to constitute part of the base from which excess profits are measured. The present resolution will exclude from standard profits those items of unusual, non-recurring income.

If a company which has
established its standard base does receive an appreciable increase in any one fiscal year, will that have to go into the one year's operating account? For instance, take Canadian Car and Foundry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They will be excluded in
the taxation year.
It will not all be. taken away from them in one year?

speechtext:
There may be some qualification as to that. I will give some consideration to it. There was an amendment last

Excess Profits Tax Act
year, if I remember correctly, relating to the extent to which that type of profit could be taken into the taxation year. The two situations should be comparable.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Is there any way in which a taxpayer can find out what is considered a fair standard profit in a certain type of industry? For instance, assume that a certain company made $10,000 in the 1936-39 period, and that company considered it a fair profit, but a competitor made 12 per cent which he considered a fair profit. He might even ask to have his standard raised to say, 15 per cent, which the board might consider a fail-profit. I wonder how that is governed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman knows, the board of referees cannot allow more than 10 per cent when capital is the determining factor. With new companies, my recollection is that the capital standard is not used, that the return is the return which is usual in the industry. It is not strictly accurate to say that the capital standard is not used; what I should have said is that the 10 per cent limit does not apply in the case of a new company. In the case of depressed companies they cannot get a standard from the board of referees which will be greater than 10 per cent on their capital; it may be considerably less. As a matter of fact, I do not know what their standard is. But the new companies are not limited to the 10 per cent, and there it is a matter for the board.
Mr. O'BRIEN: Are bank borrowings considered as capital?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the earned capital.

10. That the income of any company derived from the production of base metals or strategic minerals shall be exempt from taxation hereunder if the company first came into production during the period of three years commencing the first day of January, 1943, and such exemption shall extend to the income of the first three fiscal periods of twelve months each of any such company following commencement of such production.

Will the minister explain why the date set is January 1, 1943? It would seem that that would mean that if one of these base metal mines came into production during the present year, the company would not get the benefit of the amendment. Surely that is not the intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a continuation in a different form of the present provision. The legislation on this matter has been in existence since 1936.
Not for base metal mines, has it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Metalliferous mines.
What section of the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Section 89 of the Income War Tax Act. The present exemption applies to metalliferous mines, and that applies to mines which come into production prior to January 1, 1943. This legislation applies to mines which come into production after January 1, 1943. It widens the number of mines which are eligible, and it changes the exemption from an exemption from income tax to an exemption from excess profits tax, which would be more favourable to the companies. There is perhaps a point in that marginal number; that is, there might be some strategic minerals which will not get any assistance until after January 1, 1943. What I have said would appear to be correct from the section, but it is not correct for this reason, that there is a tuning-up period. That is to say, if a mine were discovered now, it would not be deemed to come into production until six months from now, and therefore it would come within the benefits of the proposed section.

But there are many zinc and lead mines in British Columbia which have been operated off and on for many years, going back as far as fifty years, but have been lying dormant for perhaps the last ten years. They may be brought into production this year, and it seems to me that they should get the benefit of this provision. The resolution reads in this way, that if the company first comes into production before January 1, 1943, then the company will not get the benefit of this amendment, and I suggest to* the minister that that is wrong. What we want to do is to encourage these mines to get into production as quickly as possible, and certainly from the way this resolution reads a company would be discouraged from coming into production until after the first of January, 1943. If it is intended to broaden the exemption, surely that should be dated back, say to the first of January, 1942.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is confused. There is no difference in principle between the two sections. That is, if the old mine cannot qualify now, it cannot qualify after the first of January, 1943, because it is still an old mine. What the hon. gentleman is really asking for is to extend this section from new mines to old mines which have been abandoned and are brought into production again.
Excess Profits Tax Act

No, but the way this resolution reads is, "if the company first came into production during the period of three years"; it does not say, "if 'the mine' first came into production"; it is "the company". The chances are that a mine of this type would be taken over by a new company; it would not be a matter of the old company doing the development work. It is very important that every encouragement should be given to have these mines opened up this summer. If you wait until the late fall or the winter, they cannot start in until next spring, and a whole year will be lost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may be that the resolution is wrongly worded. It is intended that the wording shall be the same and the principle shall be the same as section 89 of the Income War Tax Act. The two differences are, first, that it will extend to a wider range of mines, and second, that it will be an exemption from excess profits tax, not income tax. I should add a third, that precious metals are out.
Does the minister mean that it will apply only to the new mines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.

Well, I suggest that that is ridiculous, because the most likely place from which you will get the zinc and the lead will be from these old mines which have been partly developed. For one new mine where you would be able to get the metal there would be a hundred partly developed mines that could be developed further and from which you could get metal much faster than you could get it from a new mine. What we want here is not new mines developed so much as the ore; we want the zinc and the lead and the copper. It is not so much a matter of going out and finding new mines; it is a matter of getting the ore out where it can be found. Most of these old mines have at least some ore in them, and if encouragement is given to the owners we shall get the metal.
I suggest to the minister that this is on a wrong basis entirely, trying to open new mines. Not only does it take time to find new mines, but there are not the men to go prospecting.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And no machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The commissioner tells me that mines which have been abandoned for more than ten years and started again are ordinarily regarded as new mines. It is a matter of interpretation. The commissioner of income tax, who is administering this section, has kept in touch with the Department of Mines and Resources, but I suppose that interpretation could be changed.
IMr. Ilsley.J

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is just
an arbitrary rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The ten-year rule is arbitrary. It would not do, however, to give tax exemption for three years to a mine that had just discontinued operations for a short time. Some line would have to be drawn.
The whole purpose of this change is to get minerals for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

And to get them as quickly as possible. Perhaps if a mine has been shut down only a few months or a year, it should not get the benefit of the exemption, but to insist that it must have been closed for ten years is going too far under present conditions. This section is intended to get out the minerals, and many mines will not be helped if the restrictions are as broad as the minister has mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are giving assistance all the time to ail sorts of enterprises under one act and another and by order in council, and probably these cases could be met without laying down any general rule in an act. The metals controller is certainly doing everything he possibly can to stimulate production of the kind of metals and minerals needed in war production, and he is constantly in touch with the Department of Finance and with, the Department of National Revenue to solicit the type of assistance necessary to get the mines into operation. We have constant trouble trying to determine what degree of assistance we can defend and how far we can go. We lay down certain principles, and at times they are assailed by interested parties. One principle we laid down in the Department of Finance is that no arrangement would be made with any mining interests on the basis of which shares or bonds would be offered to the public, and we were certainly attacked for that by those interested. It was regarded as contrary to the best interests of the war effort, and so forth. The only point I am trying to make is that we are in touch with those who are closely connected with these matters, trying to get out of the earth the maximum of minerals and metals required for war production. This will be a general rule that can be applied by any statute applicable to new mines, and it carries on a principle which has been embodied in the statutes since 1936. There are just those modifications I have mentioned, such as leaving out precious metals, switching the exemption from income tax to excess profits tax, and the widening of the

class from metalliferous mines to strategic minerals not metalliferous. That is as far as we should go by legislation.

Has the government been in touch with the departments of mines in the [DOT]different mining provinces? They have a far keener appreciation of mining requirements than the dominion Department of Mines and Resources. I suggest that the Department of Finance should get in touch with the departments of mines in the different provinces and find out from them what would help most to bring about the opening up of these mines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are many good mining people in Ottawa. The metals controller, if I may say so, is a first-class official, and there are a great many good men in the Department of Mines and Resources here. We must rely on our own Department of Mines and Resources and on the metals controller and those associated with him. Both they and the national research council are doing remarkable work.

While 1 shall support the resolution, I am wondering whether the minister has gone far enough in granting assistance to new mines. I do not know the particular aspects of the problem, but I should like to say a few words to our friends *of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this regard. Here is a resolution at this late stage in the war, when we are nearly three years at war, and we have to resort to the private enterprise system and the profit motive in order to get very necessary basic materials for the war.
Because the government would not do it.

Because the government is not in a position to do it and has not the *organization; nor do I know of any government that- would be in a position to do it. They leave it to private enterprise to go ahead and get the metals out of the ground as quickly as possible and they afford some relief from taxation; but while these companies who may find the metals in the ground will be exempt from the excess profits tax, they will be subject to the 40 per cent ordinary corporation income tax and that is a very large tax in a hazardous industry. I am not giving any authoritative opinion on the matter because I have not had the facts before me, but it strikes me that 40 per cent on the profits in a hazardous industry is taking away from the industry, in the form of a tax, something that militates against the chances of that industry amounting to what it should. In the last war when there was
Excess Profits Tax Act
necessity for greater production of lead and zinc, the British government negotiated with Consolidated Smelters, which was nothing but a claim at that time. The Sullivan mine had not been successfully worked and was sold for $500,000 by the American Smelting and Refining company, to Canadian interests, because they could not produce the metal commercially. There was a metallurgical problem that to date had not been solved, and the Britilfh government said to the owners, "Get out this metal and we will take it off your hands and give you a return . That was finally done, and they got great production which was a material aid in the winning of the last war. Now we have_ a different situation, because we have price ceilings and limits to what lead and zinc can be sold for, so that there is no incentive. Moreover, we have high taxes so that private enterprise is stifled. I can say to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that if they would leave things to private enterprise, which would get things done, we would make a much greater contribution toward the war than we do by trying to change the whole economic fabric of the nation at a time when its very life is at stake.

Will the minister explain what the tax will be, first of all, on a company which comes into production in 1942 and then on a company which comes into production in 1943? As I understand it, a company coming into production in 1942 will be exempt from income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
And one coming into production in 1943 will have to pay income tax but will be exempt from excess profits tax. Is that the position? Will the minister explain the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The one that comes into production in 1942 will pay a minimum of 22 per cent, because a company is liable under the Excess Profits Tax Act to 22 per cent of the total profits, or 75 per cent of the excess, whichever is the greater. The minimum which that company will pay is 22 per cent.

That is even with the
exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is right. That is only an exemption from the income tax, which is 18 per cent. The company is still liable to the excess profits tax, and the minimum is 22 per cent. The company which comes into production in 1943 will be exempt from excess profits tax, therefore will pay only the income tax, which is 18 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So there is not much difference.

If the government really wants base metals there will have to be more than an exemption from taxation of prospective operations. There are a dozen mines in the Kaslo-Slocan district that have yielded millions of dollars in lead, zinc and silver, but the majority of those properties have been abandoned so far as operations are concerned because it has been unprofitable to operate them, because prices have been so low. The one plant in British Columbia to-day which is treating lead and1 zinc ores is paying a price so low that the average miner could not possibly operate. Lead and zinc are being supplied to the British empire by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company at a price lower than has been in force for an average of any ten years, in Canadian history. That lead and zinc is all going to the British government to-day. Before renewed operations can be undertaken, those mines must have the old timbers removed because they are rotten and1 it would not be safe to operate. There must be more than exemption from taxation. There must be a public mill or government mill which will take care of all the ores and concentrate them. The Reconstruction Finance Corporation in the United States wants Canadian lead and zinc ores, wants them so badly that I think it will be found that within the last month or so there has been a notice that the Metals Reserve Corporation proposes to erect a $100,000 mill to take care of some lead and' zinc ores which are so close to the border that there is not a railway there, but apparently they are going to carry them by truck to the United States.
The government should give serious thought to the construction of a public concentration plant. It would be the greatest incentive for the various local mines to resume operations. You cannot get capital-that is all there is to it to work lead and zinc ores to-day at the prices which now prevail in Canada. There is no capital to take hold of these industries. The incentive would be to secure the operation of a number of these smaller properties by miners who operate largely under lease and royalty, and the only way whereby they can be encouraged to do so is by the construction of a public mill and concentrator.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee to take No. 90a, b, c and d together?
Agreed.

All these four items
appear to me to be identical in present rate and past rate. Why are they inserted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only change is in item 90c. The words "extracts or" are being dropped. The wording under item 90c was:
Vegetable extracts or juices, liquid mustards, soy and vegetable sauces of all kinds.
The words "extracts or" are deleted. It would appear from the former wording that vegetable extracts might be synonymous with juices, although the rulings of the Department of National Revenue have not been made on this basis, nor is there any information before that department which would indicate that this was the intention. According to dictionary definitions the words "vegetable extracts" could apply to aqueous or alcoholic products extracted from herbs, roots and seeds, such as are used in the manufacture of ginger or herbal beverages. Such extracts, however, have always been rated under tariff item 711 or 220. Ever since the item became effective on May 2, 1930, the wording of item 90c has been more or less contradictory in the fact that the general heading of the item is "vegetables, prepared or preserved", while item 90c covers commodities which, with the exception of vegetable juices and possibly soy, do not appear to come within the category of vegetables.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The
intention, then, is to clarify a position which heretofore has been rather ambiguous?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But there is no change?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Items agreed to.
Customs tariff-152b. Orange juice, grapefruit juice, and blended orange and grapefruit juice, the product of the British West Indies, when imported direct from the countrv of production: British preferential tariff, free.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is
this? Are you taking off the 15 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is a new item, to
replace tariff items 152b and 152d by a single item, which is enlarged to cover blended orange and grapefruit juice. Blended orange
and grapefruit juice was formerly dutiable as "fruit juices, n.o.p.", at rates of 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 25 per cent. This item applies to imports under the British preferential tariff only.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And
direct importations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Tariff item 152b provided
for duty-free entry under the British preferential tariff of orange juice, the product of the British West Indies, when imported direct from the country of production. Item 152d provided for duty-free entry under the British preferential tariff of grapefruit juice, the product of the British West Indies, when imported direct from the country of production. The intermediate and general tariff rates of 25 per cent in item 152, the item covering "fruit juices, n.o.p", applies to imports of orange juice and grapefruit juice from intermediate and general tariff countries. The United States trade agreement rate on fruit juices, n.o.p., not including lime, orange, lemon or passion fruit juice, of 15 per cent applied since January 1, 1939. Imports of orange juice are not separately recorded. Imports of grapefruit juice during the period from April 1 to December 1, 1939, amounted to 1,038,756 gallons, valued at $390,808. The United States supplied 931,000 gallons, valued at $350,005. Imports from Trinidad amounted to 106,725 gallons, valued at $40,452. In 1941, imports of grapefruit juice from all countries exceeded two and a half million gallons, valued at over $972,000. Over 80 per cent of these imports came from the United States, with about 418,000 gallons valued at $198,000 coming from Trinidad. In the past, imports of blended orange and grapefruit juice have been small, owing to the tariff situation. The object of the item is to provide that blended orange and grapefruit juice will get the same rate that orange juice got and that grapefruit juice got. By blending them they forfeited the privilege of the rate which would have applied to either one unblended.

Is the subsidy being
paid on any of them now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; the subsidy on grapefruit juice was discontinued, and, if I remember correctly, that is the only juice on which it was paid.

What has this to
do with the commodities we produce in British Columbia, such as tomato juice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as I know it has
nothing whatever to do with tomato juice.
Customs Tarifj

I am sincere about this; I do not intend to be scoffed at by anyone. This country, and particularly British Columbia, produces a great deal of tomato juice, and I want to know why grapefruit juice should be brought in here when we have tomato juice available.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The proposal is to give the same tariff treatment to blended orange and grapefruit juice as is given to orange juice and grapefruit juice coming in unblended. They were both free under the British preferential tariff. Blended orange and grapefruit juice is now to be free under the same tariff.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And
formerly the blend was not free?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then what
will be the position with respect to all these items; that is, orange juice, grapefruit juice and blended orange and grapefruit juice, coming from the United States? This item is referable only to these commodities when they are the produce of the British West Indies, when imported direct from the country of origin. Of course now there is no such importation at all; there is no transportation from the countries of origin, because all the ships are gone, so this is meaningless at the moment. What is the position with respect to United States products?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been, I understand, considerable leniency in the enforcement of the rule that they must come by direct shipment-that is a national revenue matter, not a finance matter-so they may continue to come via the United States and still obtain the benefit of this free preferential rate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because of present conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The rate against United States products of this kind is 25 per cent.
Under another item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, another item altogether.
I suppose the government has to pay duty on the grapefruit juice and other products imported for use by the army, or is that not done?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the government itself import grapefruit juice which is supplied to the army, or does it buy it from contractors? I should not suppose the government would be in the business of

importing grapefruit juice for anybody. I think the government would buy in the open market, just as I would.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know; I suppose they buy it in the open market. I do not know whether or not that grapefruit juice paid duty when it came in. If it came in under these British preferential items, it would not.
Of course it might come from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, in which event it must have paid the duty.

I think the Minister of Munitions and Supply once told us that everything he imported from the United States paid the duty, where it was dutiable. I was wondering whether the Department of National Revenue or the Department of Finance had even an estimate of the total amount of duty paid by the crown for purchases of grapefruit juice and other fruit juices on behalf of the army, and perhaps for other services as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it is separately estimated at all.

I understand we brought in 30,000 gallons of grapefruit juice for the Canadian army either last year or last month. Did we pay duty on that?
' Mr. ILSLEY: If it was a product of the United States it must have paid duty when it came in; the duty must be included in the price. If it was a product of the British West Indies it probably did not.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-210. Peroxide of soda; silicate of soda, dry or in water solution; bichromate of soda; sulphite of sodium; nitrite of soda; arseniate, biarseniate, chlorate, bisulphite and stannate of soda, prussiate of soda and sulphite of soda: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, 15 per cent; general tariff, 20 per cent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the change here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only change made is that the words "silicate of soda in crystals or in solution" are amended to read, "silicate of soda, dry or in water solution".

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is there
any change in the rate?
The tariff is changed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were two rates shown in the column "present rates". The solid material was ruled to be dutiable under item

Customs Tariff
711, which is the basket item. The amended wording is for the purpose Of preventing this. The amended wording takes the old rates of free, 15 per cent and 20 per cent, and makes them apply to the solid material as well as to the material in solution. The Department of National Revenue ruled that the solid material was not covered by the section and therefore it went into the basket item and took the rates shown in the second line in the column, "present rates". There is really no change in rate, it is just a change in wording.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-276. Cotton seed oil for canning fish:	British preferential, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What are we to gather from the two different rates under the heading "present rates"? I presume that.most of this oil comes from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I think it does.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is the effect of this change?
Mr. ILSLEY; The present tariff item 276 provides for duty-free entry from all countries of refined cotton seed oils, edible, for canning fish. The wording of this item is being widened to cover unrefined cotton seed oil for canning fish.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This covers both refined and unrefined?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Have we done any refining of cotton seed oil in Canada? Has it not always been refined abroad?
Mr. ILSLEY; Sometimes they bring it in unrefined and refine it for canning fish.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-282b. Saggars, hillers, bats, and plate setters, when used in the manufacture of ceramic products: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free: general tariff, free.
Is this item intended to help the porcelain and china plants in Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. My recollection is that it allows some equipment to come in free of duty which otherwise would be dutiable. The products allowed to come in free under this item were previously dutiable under item 282a, 124, 20 and 224. It is really widening the item to provide for complete parts of saggars.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-316a. Incandescent lamp bulbs for use in the manufacture of incandescent lamps; glass tubing for use in the manufacture of incandescent lamps, vials and ampoules; mantle stocking for gas light: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, 74 per cent; general tariff, 10 per cent.

What is the effect of this?
Mr. ILSLEY; The present item 316a covering "incandescent lamp bulbs and glass tubing for use in the manufacture of incandescent lamps, and mantle stocking for gas light", with rates of free, 74 per cent and 10 per cent, is being reworded to include glass tubing for use in the manufacture of vials and ampoules. Glass tubing for the manufacture of vials and ampoules is dutiable at present under tariff item 326a at rates of 10 per cent, 20 per cent and 224 per cent, with a United States Trade agreement rate of 174 per cent. The effect of this amendment is to reduce the rate on glass tubing imported from the United States for the manufacture of vials and ampoules from 174 per cent to 74 per cent. The manufacture of vials and ampoules is a new industry in Canada, and it is estimated that imports of glass tubing for this use will range from 80,000 to 100,000 pounds annually. The average value of this tubing is about 25 cents a pound.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-349c.	Magnesium scrap:
British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.
Provided, that nothing shall be deemed to be magnesium scrap except waste or refuse magnesium fit only to be remelted.

What amount was
imported last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very little, if any.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it anticipated that this will bring it in?
We are making an effort to manufacture magnesium metal in Canada, and previously there was a substantial duty against scrap coming in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rate shown under present rates are 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 25 per cent.
Those rates are reduced to free. I have no objection because this is needed for war purposes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
